<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing of lightweight metallic alloys, particularly aluminum- and titanium-based systems, has emerged as a transformative approach for producing high-performance components with unprecedented design freedom. Among available technologies, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) offers superior geometrical resolution and microstructural control; however, the successful processing of lightweight alloys remains constrained by fundamental challenges related to printability, defect formation, and microstructural heterogeneity. This review critically examines the process–structure–property relationships governing L-PBF fabrication of aluminum and titanium alloys, with a specific focus on the mechanisms of defect generation and their implications for mechanical performance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>First, the unique thermophysical characteristics of lightweight alloys—including high reflectivity, oxidation tendency, and rapid solidification kinetics—are analyzed in the context of melt pool dynamics and thermal gradients. Second, alloy-specific microstructural evolution is discussed, highlighting the formation of cellular structures in Al–Si systems and martensitic transformations in Ti–6Al–4 V, alongside their dependence on process parameters. Third, the dominant defect mechanisms, including lack-of-fusion porosity, keyhole-induced voids, hydrogen gas porosity, and hot cracking, are systematically compared between aluminum and titanium alloys, establishing clear cause–effect relationships between processing conditions and structural integrity.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Building upon these insights, the review integrates recent advances in computational modeling approaches—such as CALPHAD, phase-field simulations, and machine learning—to demonstrate how predictive frameworks can guide alloy design and process optimization. A cross-material comparison is further developed to identify critical differences and shared limitations in printability and performance. Finally, a unified design strategy is proposed, linking process control, alloy chemistry, and defect mitigation to enable the development of next-generation lightweight materials tailored for additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This work provides a focused and analytical perspective that bridges fundamental mechanisms with practical design strategies, offering a roadmap for advancing lightweight alloy applications in aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors.</jats:p>

The excerpt does not report measured thermal-conductivity values for a loose aluminium powder bed. It gives the AS61 aluminium powder’s tap porosity as ΘM = 0.45 and lists a fitted parameter κ0 = 231.71 W/(m·K), obtained from fitting thermal-conductivity data for sintered compacts—not from a loose powder-bed measurement. The study’s aluminium compacts covered a final porosity range of 0.01–0.32, so this excerpt does not provide a direct value at the loose-bed condition (approximately the tap porosity). For comparison, the excerpt states that the literature thermal conductivity of fully dense pure aluminium is 238 W/(m·K). Thus, based solely on the supplied text, a quantitative reduction of loose-bed effective conductivity relative to solid aluminium cannot be calculated. The available κ0 value is only about 6.29 W/(m·K), or approximately 2.64%, below 238 W/(m·K), but it should not be interpreted as the loose powder-bed conductivity.

Thermal De-coating Pre-treatment for Loose or Compacted Aluminum Scrap and Consequences for Salt-Flux Recycling Valid Text Names: 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 1-3', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 3-4', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 4-6', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 6-8', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 8-10', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 10-11', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 11-12', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 12-13' BibTex: @article{vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment, author = "Vallejo-Olivares, Alicia and Høgåsen, Solveig and Kvithyld, Anne and Tranell, Gabriella", title = "Thermal De-coating Pre-treatment for Loose or Compacted Aluminum Scrap and Consequences for Salt-Flux Recycling", year = "2022", journal = "Journal of Sustainable Metallurgy", volume = "8", pages = "1485-1497", month = "Oct", doi = "10.1007/s40831-022-00612-x", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-022-00612-x", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "4", issn = "2199-3823" } Abstract: In aluminum recycling, thermal de-coating pre-treatments remove moisture and organic contamination before re-melting. If the scrap is compacted into bales or briquettes before the thermal treatment and re-melting processes, less surface area is exposed to oxidation in contact with air. However, compaction may also limit the efficiency of the de-coating process. In this study, coated sheets of aluminum were thermally de-coated at varied temperatures and durations. Observations of changes in coating thickness, mass, color, and composition revealed a maximum de-coating efficiency of close to 75% wt due to remaining oxide residues. The relationship between de-coating and compaction was investigated by thermally treating loose shreddings (chips) and briquettes of various densities. The briquettes were compacted by three methods: uniaxial, moderate-pressure torsion (MPT), and MPT at 450 °C (Hot MPT); and the de-coating efficiency was calculated from the mass loss. Subsequently, the samples were re-melted under salt-flux and compared with another set of samples which were re-melted without thermal pre-treatment. The results showed that thermal de-coating significantly promotes the coalescence of loose chips and briquettes compacted uniaxially, up to similar coalescences than initially uncoated aluminum samples. Thermally treating the MPT briquettes, which were more densely compacted, led to less de-coating, and subsequently lower coalescences. The analysis of re-melted material revealed that the coating residues did not significantly affect the composition, while the compaction prevented Mg loss for the uncoated materials. The objective was to assess the density, porosity, chemical composition, and metallurgical yield of the briquettes before and after melting, as well as to determine their suitability for use as deoxidizing additives in steelmaking. The cold-pressed briquette (Sample A) exhibited a low density of 2.29 g.cm-³ and a porosity of 12.1%, resulting from intergranular voids and residual lubricants. After melting and resolidification (Sample B), the density increased to 2.388 g.cm-3 and the porosity decreased to 8.15%. XRF chemical analysis confirmed a high degree of elemental homogeneity after melting with no indication of segregation, while SEM–EDS microstructural analysis verified the absence of significant intermetallic phases and revealed only a thin surface oxide layer. The metallurgical yield reached 94.2% with a low dross content (2.25%). Effects of Compaction and Thermal Pre-treatments on Generation of Dross and Off-Gases in Aluminium Recycling Valid Text Names: 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 1-3', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 3-4', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 4-6', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 6-8', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 8-11', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 11-12', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 12-13', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 13-14', 'vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 14-14' BibTex: @article{vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction, author = "Vallejo-Olivares, Alicia and Gertjegerdes, Tom and Høgåsen, Solveig and Friedrich, Bernd and Tranell, Gabriella", title = "Effects of Compaction and Thermal Pre-treatments on Generation of Dross and Off-Gases in Aluminium Recycling", year = "2023", journal = "Journal of Sustainable Metallurgy", volume = "10", pages = "69-82", month = "Dec", doi = "10.1007/s40831-023-00773-3", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-023-00773-3", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "1", issn = "2199-3823" } Abstract: Organic coatings are a challenge for aluminium packaging recycling since they tend to increase the re-melting metal losses. A solution is de-coating the scrap via a thermal pre-treatment to burn-off the organics before re-melting. Due to logistic benefits, the scrap is often pressed into bales. This study evaluates the influence of compaction on the de-coating efficiency and off-gas emissions, and its consequences for dross formation and recycling metal yield. Loose chips and two types of briquettes, one loosely compacted by uniaxial pressure and the other compacted by moderated-pressure-torsion to higher densities, were heated to 550 °C while analysing the off-gas emissions using FTIR. The briquettes were subsequently re-melted into a molten heel. Re-melting coated scrap multiplied the % wt of dross by a factor of 2 or 3, depending on the compaction pre-treatment, compared to re-melting uncoated aluminium. The densest briquettes emitted less than half the CO2 and CO gases during de-coating and formed significantly more dross. Compaction to the lower densities showed no tangible effects. The effect of de-coating compacted materials or not was small (± 2% wt dross), which was attributed to carbonaceous residues remaining after the thermal treatment. In conclusion, high compactions by torsion limit the de-coating reactions, which depend on factors such as temperature and gas transport. A complete removal of the organic residues is critical for a more sustainable recycling with less dross generated. From text 'baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20'.

Petr Baron, Jozef Mikita, and Vladimír Simkulet. Characterization of cold-pressed aluminum briquettes and their behavior during remelting for application in steel deoxidation. Unknown journal, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1, doi:10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1.

The excerpt reports remelting performance for compacted aluminium briquettes, particularly Sample B. Its post-remelting density was 2.388 g·cm⁻³, with a dross fraction of 2.25%, relative melting loss of 3.55%, and metallurgical yield of 94.2%. The authors place this result within the expected 90–96% yield range for briquettes with densities around 2.15–2.40 g·cm⁻³, and identify 2.20–2.40 g·cm⁻³ as an optimal density range for steel deoxidation. The excerpt directly addresses the steam-explosion hazard when water or moisture is trapped within or enclosed by molten aluminum. In cited aluminum–water experiments, violent explosions required liquid water to become enclosed by a compact mass of aluminum and an aluminum temperature high enough to cause rapid, essentially explosive water vaporization, followed by rapid oxidation of the newly formed metal particles. Thus, wet, porous, or otherwise gas- or moisture-containing aluminum added to molten aluminum could create a sudden steam-generation and molten-metal dispersal event if the moisture is confined and heat transfer is rapid. The severity depends on the quantity of simultaneously reacting metal, the specific surface area of particles, metal temperature, water depth, stream geometry, and whether the metal forms a compact mass. Conditions that cool or disperse the aluminum reduce the likelihood of the described violent mechanism, while high temperature and confinement promote it. The passage does not specifically discuss hydrogen evolution, hydrated oxide decomposition, trapped non-water gas expansion, or oxide hydration during remelting, although it notes uncertainty about participating reactions and identifies rapid oxidation as part of the explosion sequence. It also indicates that molten-metal dispersal itself may be significant in reactor environments.

Abstract:
Selected laser melting (SLM) is a representative process of powder-bed type 3D printing technology that is used to manipulate metals and it generally results in various structural properties according to the process conditions. In this study, a thermal conductivity test was conducted on AlSi10Mg specimens that were manufactured using the SLM process to investigate the influence of various process conditions on the thermophysical characteristics and cellular microstructure of the samples. The building direction of the specimen, laser scan speed, and hatch spacing were considered as process variables, and the thermal conductivity was analyzed for each process variable. In the test results, as the polar angle of the specimen increased from 0° to 90°, the thermal conductivity increased. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity gradually decreased as the scan speed and hatch spacing increased. The differences in thermal characteristics are discussed in connection with the microstructure of the cells constituting the melt pool. The solidified melt pool that formed by the laser beam is composed of cells consisting of an Al matrix and a surrounding Si-rich area. The differences in thermal conductivity of the overall specimens are explained based on the variations in thermal conductivity and cell shape and size for each chemical component.

Abstract:
Ce projet a ete entrepris pour etudier les interactions entre les particules d'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions sous des conditions d'ecoulement de l'aluminium liquide. Le but du projet etait de developper une methode d'essai qui permet de simuler les conditions similaires a celles dans le procede de filtration d'aluminium et d'evaluer les interactions qui ont lieu entre les differents types d'echantillons d'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions. Cette methode d'essai avait pour but de determiner commenles differents types d'alumine se comportent durant le procede de filtration.
 
Les interactions chimiques entre l'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions ont ete etudiees dans des conditions d'ecoulement statiques et dynamique. Afin d'etudier ces interactions dans des conditions d'ecoulement dynamique, la connaissance du champ de vitesse au voisinage des particules d'alumine est necessaire. Dans ce projet, deux systemes experimentaux uniques qui peuvent simuler l'ecoulement dans le lit du filtre industriel ont ete concus et construits. Un modele mathematique a ete developpe pour predire le champ d'ecoulement autour des particules dans le systeme experimental. Le modele mathematique a ete valide en comparant les predictions avec les resultats d'un modele physique dans lequel l'eau etait utilisee comme fluide. Ensuite, le modele mathematique a ete utilise pour effectuer des etudes parametriques afin de determiner les parametres de design et d'operation pour le systeme experimental actuel dans lequel les tests ont ete faits. Cela a permis de generer un champ d'ecoulement similaire a celui du filtre industriel.
 
Des experiences avec divers alliages d'aluminium-magnesium liquide (0, 2, 5 et 7% Mg, en poids) ont ete realisees pour des differents temps de residence (de 6 heures a 168 heures) en utilisant les systemes experimentaux decrits ci-hauts. Les effets de la vitesse de l'alliage d'aluminium liquide, de la temperature du liquide, des proprietes physiques (porosite apparente, la rugosite de la surface, etc.) et chimiques (teneur en impuretes telles que Na2O, SiO2, etc.) sur le degre des reactions interfaciales entre l'alliage d'aluminium et l'alumine ont ete determines.
 
Les echantillons obtenus des experiences aluminium-alumina ont ete analyses a l'aide du microscope optique, du microscope electronique a balayage - la spectroscopie aux rayons X a dispersion d'energie (MEB-EDX), du microprobe MEB, et de la diffraction des rayons X (DRX). Les resultats montrent que les reactions chimiques entre l'alpha-alumine pure a haute densite et les alliages Mg-Al liquides ne sont pas rapide; mais, la presence des impuretes (telle que Na2O en tant que phase de beta-alumine) et la structure poreuse de l'alumine augmentent l'etendue des reactions significativement. La phase riche en Na2O (beta-alumine) qui se trouve dans toutes les alumines commerciales semble etre l'un des facteurs les plus importants pour les reactions spontanees avec la vapeur de magnesium, meme au temps de residence le plus court. Mg-spinelle a ete trouve comme le produit de reaction le plus important. L'analyse thermodynamique indique la meme tendance.

This project was undertaken to study the interactions between alumina particles, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions under liquid aluminum flow conditions. The objective was to develop a test method which can simulate the conditions similar to those in the aluminum filtration process and to evaluate the interactions taking place between various types of alumina samples, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions. With this test method, it was aimed to determine how various alumina types behave under flow conditions during the filtration process.
 
Chemical interactions between alumina, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions were investigated under both static and dynamic flow conditions. In order to study these interactions under dynamic flow conditions, a knowledge of the velocity field in the vicinity of the alumina particles is necessary. In this project, two unique experimental systems which can simulate the flow condition of the industrial bed were designed and built. A mathematical model was also developed to predict the flow field around the particles in the experimental system. The mathematical model was validated by comparing the predictions with the results from a physical model in which water was used as the fluid. The mathematical model was then used to conduct parametric studies to determine the design and operational parameters for the actual experimental system in which the tests were carried out. This allowed the generation of a flow field similar to that of the industrial filter.
 
The experiments with various liquid Mg-Al alloys (0, 2, 5, and 7 wt% Mg) were conducted for different residence times (from 6 hours to 168 hours) using the above experimental systems. The effects of the liquid aluminum alloy velocity, the temperature of the melt, the physical (apparent porosity, surface roughness, etc.) and chemical (impurity content such as Na2O, SiO2 etc.) properties of alumina samples on the extent of aluminum alloy/alumina interfacial reactions were determined.
 
The samples obtained from aluminum-alumina experiments were analyzed by using the optical microscope, the scanning electron microscope - energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX), the micro probe SEM, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results indicate that the chemical reactions between high density pure alpha-alumina and molten Mg-Al alloys are not fast; however, the presence of impurities (such as Na20 as beta alumina phase) and the porous structure in alumina increase the extent of reactions significantly. Na2O rich phase (beta alumina) found in all commercial alumina grades seems to be one of the most important contributors for the spontaneous reactions of Mg vapor with alumina, even at the shortest residence time. The major reaction product was found to be Mg-spinel. The thermodynamic analysis indicated the same tendency.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 4-5'.

V. Yu. Bazhin, S. A. Savchenkov, and Ya. I. Kosov. Specificity of the titanium-powder alloying tablets usage in aluminium alloys. ArXiv, pages 52-56, Dec 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11, doi:10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt reports that titanium alloying tablets or briquettes dissolve effectively in aluminium melt, with titanium assimilation to 0.20% taking no more than 40 minutes for specimens from different suppliers. The fastest dissolution was 28 minutes for a briquette containing molasses. Initial sampling after 5–7 minutes showed only a small titanium increase because transfer from the tablet surface was slow. After briquette breakup, titanium content increased rapidly. Tablet porosity is identified as a key factor: sufficient interconnected porosity allows molten aluminium to penetrate the compact and interact actively with titanium particles until complete dissolution. This implies that overconsolidated or excessively dense briquettes can hinder melt penetration and slow dissolution, although the excerpt does not provide a quantified density–dissolution relationship. Stirring, or using the alloying element in dispersed form, is recommended to accelerate melt saturation. Dissolution also occurs under free or forced convection, with isothermal holding time and selected melt temperature affecting the process, but no specific temperature values are given here. Molasses improves flux adhesion to titanium powder and strengthens the tablets during pressing; the figure compares porosity backgrounds with and without molasses. Listed tablet densities range approximately from 3.28 to 4.12 g/cm³, alongside mechanical strength ratings, but these data are not directly correlated with dissolution time.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 2-4'.

V. Yu. Bazhin, S. A. Savchenkov, and Ya. I. Kosov. Specificity of the titanium-powder alloying tablets usage in aluminium alloys. ArXiv, pages 52-56, Dec 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11, doi:10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt identifies compact density and porosity as major controls on titanium alloying-tablet dissolution in aluminium melt. The recommended tablet density is 2.5–5.0 g/cm3, obtained at an optimum compaction pressure of 250–300 kg/cm2 (25.5–29.8 MPa). Excessive pressure, 350–500 kg/cm2, can fracture titanium powder particles internally. During melting, aluminium can penetrate these voids, allowing flux–metal interaction and oxide formation, which ultimately becomes slag. Overconsolidated briquettes have insufficient porosity, so the moving aluminium melt cannot infiltrate them fully; they may form a barrier oxide layer and dissolve slowly, with a reported dissolution rate of 35–40 minutes. Conversely, pressures of 100–200 kg/cm2 fail to provide adequate density and strength, causing crumbling and losses of tablet geometry exceeding 5–15%. Irregular, high-surface-area titanium particles are preferred because they compact at relatively low pressure while retaining the porosity and strength needed for melt absorption. Molasses improves flux adhesion, particle cohesion, and tablet strength; annealing at 80–100 °C burns out 50–60% of the binder while retaining porosity and strength. The excerpt does not provide specific effects of melt stirring or temperature on dissolution time beyond the annealing conditions, nor does it give a separate quantitative dissolution time for optimally compacted tablets.

The excerpt provides useful experimental information for studying compact or tablet interaction with molten aluminium, although it does not directly report alloying-tablet dissolution times, titanium powder tablets, flux effects, or overconsolidated briquette dissolution problems. Laboratory alumina tablets were deliberately manufactured with differing impurity contents while maintaining similar physical properties, allowing chemical composition effects to be isolated. The tablets used high-purity tabular and calcined alumina powders with additions of silica, soda ash, and magnesium oxide. Polyvinyl alcohol binder was added to improve green strength, and the mixture was pressed at 30 tons into 32 mm diameter, 10 mm thick discs, then dried and sintered at 1600°C for five hours. ## pqac-00000041

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 86-92'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes aluminum SPS as a process that promotes particle bonding by overcoming the native oxide film covering each aluminum particle. Aluminum is difficult to sinter conventionally because its stable oxide layer persists at high temperature and limits oxide solubility, producing a long incubation period. Successful sintering therefore requires the oxide films to be disrupted so that clean metal-to-metal contacts can form. SPS combines uniaxial pressure with pulsed direct current and Joule heating in a conductive graphite die. Localized heating at particle interfaces, together with plastic deformation during compaction, is proposed to facilitate oxide-layer fracture or breakdown. High-temperature contact points in SPS/PECS favor oxide disruption more effectively than conventional hot pressing. Pressure contributes by deforming particles, increasing contact area, breaking or displacing oxide films, and enabling stronger metallurgical bonds. Studies cited in the excerpt associate higher pressure at elevated temperature with improved ductility, neck growth, and more uniform sintering. Oxide debris generated during SPS can also improve metal-to-metal contact. The abstract further reports that electrical resistance drops markedly near 0.3 Tm; the area under this drop correlates with ductility, interpreted as evidence that oxide breakdown becomes easier and metallurgical bonding improves at this temperature. Overall, SPS oxide disruption results from the combined effects of current-assisted interfacial heating, pressure-driven plastic deformation, and formation of intimate metallic contacts.

## pqac-00000042

The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum as a coupled mechanical and electrical-thermal process. Compaction pressure is considered the primary mechanism: plastic deformation of aluminum particles fractures or disrupts their oxide layers, allowing improved metal-to-metal contact and interface bonding. Increasing pressure from 20 to 50 MPa increased final density, produced near-full density at 50 MPa, and improved ductility, supporting the importance of pressure-driven oxide breakup and contact formation. The applied electrical current enhances this process through Joule self-heating within the powder bed. Localized high temperatures at particle contacts soften the aluminum, making pressure-induced deformation more effective, while electrical-field effects may independently assist oxide disruption. The excerpt also notes that pressure ramping during heating can improve ductility compared with applying constant pressure before heating. This may result from greater electrical-field exposure at lower initial powder density, increased atomic mobility and diffusion, enhanced spark formation or local heating between particles, and reduced gas entrapment. A marked resistance decrease near 200 °C is interpreted as evidence of oxide-layer breakdown and is used to assess the quality of interfaces between aluminum particles. Thus, oxide fracture during compaction is not attributed to pressure alone; pressure, current-assisted heating, local contact conditions, and evolving particle interfaces act together.

The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum powder as primarily a mechanically driven process. Aluminum particles possess an inherent oxide layer, and plastic deformation during compaction can fracture or disrupt this film, enabling metal-to-metal contact and particle bonding. Applied pressure is therefore critical: increasing pressure produces greater oxide disruption, more consolidated metal contacts, reduced porosity, higher flexural strength and ductility, and more pronounced dimples on fracture surfaces. At low pressure, particle debonding and limited neck development remain visible; at higher pressure, prior particle boundaries diminish and ductile dimple formation increases. Electrical resistance provides indirect evidence of oxide breakdown and contact formation. Resistance decreases as densification progresses, with a particularly significant reduction near 0.3 Tm, coinciding with enhanced densification and interpreted as increased metal-to-metal bonding after oxide-layer disruption. The oxide film becomes easier to break at elevated temperature, especially above approximately 200 °C, because aluminum softens relative to alumina. Current application is considered to amplify the pressure effect through Joule heating within the powder bed, promoting plastic deformation and oxide fracture. SPS can disrupt the oxide layer and produce good bonding, particularly for inert-gas-atomized aluminum with a relatively thin oxide layer (approximately 3–4 nm), whereas air-atomized powder has a thicker layer (approximately 7 nm) and is more difficult to bond. Increasing oxide thickness reduces the likelihood of sufficient metal-to-metal contact during SPS. Applied pressure or load is important because it promotes particle contact and oxide breakup; in alloy powders containing Mg, a possible Mg–alumina spinel layer may require a higher load to fracture the oxide. ## pqac-00000047

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt identifies the native aluminum oxide film as the principal barrier to powder sintering because it prevents diffusion and metal-to-metal contact between particles. Oxide disruption can occur through several mechanisms: plastic deformation during powder compaction, formation of a liquid phase, cracking during heating, and reactions involving magnesium that produce MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel. However, the mechanical disruption produced by conventional compaction pressure is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering. This implies that pressure may create discontinuities or cracks in the oxide network, but does not normally break it up enough to achieve reliable bonding by itself. Successful aluminum powder sintering therefore often relies on liquid-phase penetration through defects formed during compaction, with suitable wetting and mass transport. Magnesium can further assist by reducing or disrupting the oxide and enabling liquid penetration. In relation to SPS, the excerpt states that pulsed current may provide electropulsing-related benefits, including refined microstructure and potentially improved mechanical properties. It also reports that SPS of pure aluminum has produced good particle bonding by reducing the oxide-layer problem, although bonding difficulties remain possible for some aluminum alloys. The passage does not provide a quantitative pressure dependence or a detailed SPS-specific fracture model.

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000049

From text 'wu2022meltrefiningand pages 4-6'.

Jianxin Wu, Faramarz Djavanroodi, Ceren Gode, Shokouh Attarilar, and Mahmoud Ebrahimi. Melt refining and purification processes in al alloys: a comprehensive study. Materials Research Express, 9:032001, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03, doi:10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03. This article has 78 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses hydrogen and oxide/non-metallic inclusion removal during aluminium melt treatment, although it does not specifically discuss powder or scrap remelting, casting-quality defects, bifilms, or passage through a small orifice/nozzle. Hydrogen and inclusions can be reduced by flotation or rotary degassing: inert or chemically inactive gases such as argon or nitrogen are introduced as fine bubbles, hydrogen diffuses into the bubbles and is removed at the melt surface, while suspended inclusions attach to rising bubbles and float out. Small bubbles are particularly useful because their high surface-area-to-volume ratio promotes hydrogen transfer and can also remove non-metallic solid particles. Enhanced melt flow improves bubble–inclusion collisions, inclusion agglomeration, and purification. Filtration removes contaminants, trapped oxides, and other second-phase particles as molten aluminium passes through refractory beds, screens, or ceramic foam filters. The stated target particle size range is 1–30 μm. Cake filtration mainly separates larger inclusions, whereas bed filtration removes particles through collision, adhesion, sedimentation, and fluid-dynamic effects. Filter performance depends on porosity, roughness, area, bed length, melt temperature, and flow rate. Bonded ceramic filters reportedly achieve up to 90% removal for 10–25 μm inclusions, while high-porosity ceramic foam filters are more effective for finer particles.


---

## pqac-00000050

From text 'schlesinger2006aluminumrecycling pages 47-51'.

Mark E. Schlesinger. Aluminum Recycling. CRC Press, Nov 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420006247, doi:10.1201/9781420006247.

The excerpt is a bibliography for a chapter on metal refining and purification rather than a discussion of experimental results. It identifies several directly relevant sources concerning hydrogen and oxide/nonmetallic inclusions in molten aluminum, especially where melt quality affects casting performance. Hydrogen measurement and removal are represented by studies comparing hydrogen-testing methods, assessing hydrogen in 319 alloy using thermal analysis, and evaluating in-line degassing and gas-fluxing systems. Inclusion formation, identification, sampling, and cleanliness are covered by references on inclusions in foundry alloys, particulate detection using LiMCA, LAIS sampling, and evaluation of molten-metal cleanliness for high-integrity die castings. The bibliography also contains extensive material on filtration, including ceramic-foam, bonded-particle, rigid-media, fiberglass-fabric, deep-bed, and cartridge filters, as well as industrial filtration performance and removal of molten-salt inclusions. Several entries concern secondary or recycled aluminum and therefore may be useful for remelting scrap, while others address fluxing, chlorine treatment, alkali/alkaline-earth removal, and degassing. However, this excerpt does not explicitly discuss powder remelting, oxide-film bifilms, inclusion-size effects at a small orifice/nozzle, or quantitative relationships between hydrogen/inclusion content and casting defects. Those topics would require consulting the cited publications or the main chapter text.


---

## pqac-00000051

From text 'wu2022meltrefiningand pages 1-3'.

Jianxin Wu, Faramarz Djavanroodi, Ceren Gode, Shokouh Attarilar, and Mahmoud Ebrahimi. Melt refining and purification processes in al alloys: a comprehensive study. Materials Research Express, 9:032001, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03, doi:10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03. This article has 78 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies hydrogen and oxide inclusions as major contaminants generated during aluminum melting. Molten aluminum reacts with oxygen and water vapor, producing aluminum oxides and dissolved hydrogen; hydrogen reportedly represents about 70%–90% of the total gas in the melt. These contaminants contribute directly to casting defects, particularly pores and slag inclusions, while inclusions and retained gas can also promote cracking, pinholes, dross, and reduced product quality. Poorly wetted non-metallic inclusions remain suspended in the melt and provide nucleation sites for porosity. Inclusions can also reduce melt fluidity and impair riser efficiency, while acting as initiation sites for pitting corrosion and degrading mechanical properties. The stated objective of melt refining is to reduce inclusions, oxides, and hydrogen to acceptable levels. The review lists fluxing, flotation, and filtration as the principal purification approaches, with method selection depending on impurity type and the required purification level. This excerpt does not provide specific data on remelted powder versus scrap, oxide bifilm formation, inclusion-size distributions, or filtration behavior through small orifices/nozzles; those topics would require later sections or other sources.


---

## pqac-00000052

From text 'wu2022meltrefiningand pages 3-4'.

Jianxin Wu, Faramarz Djavanroodi, Ceren Gode, Shokouh Attarilar, and Mahmoud Ebrahimi. Melt refining and purification processes in al alloys: a comprehensive study. Materials Research Express, 9:032001, Mar 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03, doi:10.1088/2053-1591/ac5b03. This article has 78 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses the effects of hydrogen and oxide inclusions on aluminum melt and casting-related quality. Oxide inclusions and films can act as initiation sites for pitting corrosion and, if retained in the melt, deteriorate mechanical properties, machinability, and surface quality. Common solid impurities include Al2O3, MgO, and Al4C3, while hydrogen is identified as the only dissolved gas of concern because its low solubility in aluminum promotes gas-pore formation. The article emphasizes that melt refining and purification are therefore essential, including for aluminum scrap and alloy processing. Traditional purification routes include fluxing, flotation, and filtration. Filtration can remove trapped oxides, nonmetallic inclusions, contaminants, and relatively large particles, but its effectiveness depends on filter type and it is less effective for finer inclusions; consequently, the excerpt does not provide a specific inclusion-size threshold or describe flow through a small orifice/nozzle. Fluxing can separate built-up oxides and evacuate dissolved hydrogen, while flotation reduces hydrogen and inclusions. The passage does not explicitly discuss powder remelting, oxide bifilms as a specific defect mechanism, or quantitative hydrogen/inclusion limits, but its discussion of oxide films, gas pores, inclusion retention, and filtration is relevant to those topics.


---

## pqac-00000053

From text 'koont2013intéractionentreles pages 45-50'.

Zafer Koont. Intéraction entre les particules d'alumines, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions durant la filtration d'aluminium avant la coulée. ArXiv, Jan 2013. URL: https://doi.org/10.1522/030586186, doi:10.1522/030586186. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt is highly relevant to oxide inclusions and filtration of molten aluminum, but it does not specifically address hydrogen content, remelting powder or scrap, bifilm terminology, or flow through a small orifice/nozzle. It states that inclusions can impair surface appearance, mechanical properties, machining, and forming. Inclusions are classified as exogenous, entering from ingots, alloying additions, master alloys, or refractory containment materials, and endogenous, forming through reactions in the metal-handling system such as oxidation, aluminum carbide, and halide formation. Common Al-Mg alloy inclusions include aluminum oxide films and clusters, MgO, MgAl2O4 spinel, aluminum carbide, complex oxides, and TiB2. Inclusion dimensions range from micron-scale particles to alumina films and clusters several millimeters in size, while many products require inclusions below 50 micrometers at several volume parts per million. Deep-bed filtration is described as effective for capturing inclusions below 20 micrometers because of the filter’s large surface area. Capture involves transport to filter-media sites by impingement, interception, sedimentation, diffusion, and hydrodynamic effects, followed by particle attachment through pressure, chemical, or van der Waals forces. Filter performance depends on particle size and type, approach velocity, temperature, and media characteristics.

## pqac-00000054

From text 'koont2013intéractionentreles pages 23-28'.

Zafer Koont. Intéraction entre les particules d'alumines, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions durant la filtration d'aluminium avant la coulée. ArXiv, Jan 2013. URL: https://doi.org/10.1522/030586186, doi:10.1522/030586186. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt is relevant to oxide inclusions and filtration effects on aluminium casting quality, but it does not specifically discuss hydrogen content, remelting powder or scrap, bifilms, or filtration through a small orifice/nozzle. It explains that inclusion size, shape, number, and distribution are indicators of alloy quality. Inclusions can reduce melt fluidity, increase internal porosity, alter mechanical properties, and degrade surface quality and machinability; they may also cause holes or tears in products such as thin sheets and wires. Filtration is presented as the final purification step before casting. In deep-bed filtration, molten aluminium flows through graded layers of tabular alumina, where inclusions are separated from the melt. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Method | Advantages | Disadvantages | Best suited for | Risk of nozzle clogging |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loose powder in cup (current approach) | Simple weighing; cup keeps powder together initially; convenient for composition screening. | Powder bed is thermally insulating; each particle retains a refractory oxide shell; the cup may melt before its contents coalesce, releasing floating agglomerates. Hydrous oxide, moisture, and trapped gas can evolve suddenly. Mg-bearing powder can additionally contain MgO/MgAl₂O₄. | Only low-oxide, readily melting pre-alloyed powder already demonstrated to consolidate—e.g., the successful 4047 case—and only after a separate melt test. | **High.** Oxide films and clusters can range from micrometres to millimetres, whereas the nozzle is only 0.7 mm; powder-derived Al₂O₃, MgO, or spinel may remain suspended (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000053). |
| Cold-pressed freestanding compact | Raises bulk density, thermal conductivity, strength, and probability of submergence; particle deformation cracks some oxide films. Aluminium powders reached about 94.5–97.0% relative density under load at 246–386 MPa in warm-compaction tests. | Pressing cracks but does not remove oxide; closed porosity can trap gas. Excessive density can inhibit melt infiltration, while low pressure gives weak compacts. No direct evidence guarantees complete dissolution during a 2 min hold. | Initial screening of 4047/6063 or Al-rich blends; use moderate density rather than maximum density, heat from cold beneath solid charge, and validate before atomization. | **Medium–high.** Better than loose powder, but all particle-surface oxide remains in the charge as fragments or networks; filtration literature targets inclusions as small as 1–30 µm (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049). |
| Sintered, vacuum-hot-pressed, or SPS compact | Strongest and most conductive powder-derived slug; heat plus pressure increases oxide rupture and metal-to-metal bonding. SPS at 500 °C gave 92.5–98.4% density at 20–50 MPa. Vacuum processing can desorb gas before pores close. | More equipment and process development; oxide is dispersed, not eliminated. Near-full density can retain closed gas if degassing is inadequate. Conventional sintering alone is difficult because alumina inhibits diffusion. | When powder chemistry cannot be obtained as a cast master alloy and a repeatable, mechanically robust slug is essential; vacuum hot pressing is preferable to lubricant-bearing green pressing. | **Medium.** Lower risk of releasing intact powder agglomerates, but fractured Al₂O₃/MgO/spinel remains as inclusions and can reach the nozzle (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000046). |
| Commercial master-alloy additions (e.g., Al–50Si, Al–20Si, Al–50Mg, Al–50Cu) | Cast metallic pieces melt or dissolve much more predictably than powder; low surface-area-to-volume ratio minimizes oxide introduced per gram of alloying element. Al–50Si has been used experimentally to make Al–1Si through Al–8Si melts at 850 °C. | Limited available chemistries and minimum order quantities; mass additions become small for trace targets; volatile Mg still needs controlled handling, and high-solute master alloys can segregate if incompletely dissolved. | **Preferred route** for Si, Mg, Cu and other elements available in suitable master alloys, especially for 100–350 g charges requiring low oxygen and short processing time. | **Low**, provided pieces are clean, dry, completely dissolved, and the melt is sampled before pouring (pqac-00000057). |
| Pre-alloyed powder or wire | Pre-alloying removes the need for long-range dissolution of separate elemental particles; wire has much less oxide area and can be submerged readily. Pre-alloyed atomization feed also gives the most reliable nominal composition. | Pre-alloyed powder still has one oxide shell per particle and may reproduce the consolidation problem; custom wire or powder can be costly. | Wire or rod for commercially available chemistries; pre-alloyed powder only if it is first consolidated or converted into a dense master button. | **Low for clean wire/rod; medium–high for powder.** Powder retains high oxide area even when chemically homogeneous (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000046). |
| Arc-melted master-alloy button | Converts a weighed powder blend into a dense, inspectable button before it enters the atomizer crucible; repeated flipping/remelting can improve button homogeneity; eliminates loose powder and most open porosity. | Requires an arc melter; Mg and other volatile elements may be lost; reactive elements may oxidize or react with the hearth; segregation and composition loss must be checked analytically. This recommendation is an engineering extrapolation rather than direct evidence from the cited aluminium-remelting studies. | Small experimental additions of Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Zr or Sc where no suitable commercial master alloy exists; especially attractive when preserving the atomizer nozzle is more important than minimizing preparation steps. | **Low–medium.** Much lower than a green compact if the button is sound and surface oxide is removed, but refractory reaction products can remain. |
| Higher superheat and longer hold time | Increases heat transfer, diffusion, and dissolution kinetics; requires no new forming equipment. Commercial Ti-powder tablets dissolved at 730–750 °C in roughly 25–40 min, showing that time can overcome some compact-dissolution limitations. | Your 810–840 °C set point is already substantially superheated; a 2 min hold is far shorter than published tablet times. Longer/hotter holding increases oxidation, hydrogen pickup, Mg loss, crucible/nozzle reactions, and cycle time. It cannot remove alumina shells. | A secondary optimization after proving complete melting; useful for dense cast master-alloy pieces, not as the primary remedy for loose powder. | **Medium–high for powder-derived charges; low for clean cast additions.** Extra time may float some inclusions but can also form more oxide (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000051). |
| Compact inside cup with vented sliding plug | Combines improved powder thermal contact with an aluminium envelope; a freely sliding, positively vented plug can maintain containment while permitting gas escape. | If the cup melts before the core, the assembly reverts to a floating compact. A press-fit or obstructed 1 mm vent can behave as a pressure vessel once molten metal seals it; moisture, hydrated oxide, or lubricant can cause rapid gas evolution and metal ejection. | Only as a staged cold-charge experiment with dry, lubricant-free powder, moderate compaction, an unobstructed vent path, and the assembly buried beneath solid feed—not dropped into an existing bath. | **Medium–high.** Better containment than loose powder, but failure of the envelope can release the compact’s oxide inventory abruptly; the safety consequence of blocked venting is also greater (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). |

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed

        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective

    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,

Use the tools to answer the question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module) and want to know whether pressing our alloying powder into a compact before melting would fix a melting and mixing problem. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), and give numbers wherever the sources have them.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated) heated by induction, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. Argon at a small overpressure (~0.2 bar), 13-20 ppm O2 in the chamber, melt set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes before pouring. Charges are 170-350 g. There is no mechanical stirring; any stirring comes from the induction field.

**Current charge.** A 6063 aluminium cup (19 mm OD, 12.7 mm bore, 57 mm deep) is filled by weight with gas-atomized alloy powder, closed with a press-fit 6063 plug that has a 1 mm vent hole, and melted with solid 6063 rod. Pieces must stay under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall. In one run the core was AlSi10Mg powder, and it did not melt into the bath: the cup melted, but the powder did not consolidate. In another run the core was 4047 (Al-12Si) powder, and it melted. Next we want composition spreads (varying how much 4047 powder goes into 6063, checked by SEM/EDS) and later blends with elemental or master-alloy powders (for example Si, Mg, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Zr, Sc). The problem is that the powder struggles to melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt in the time and temperature available. The equipment maker warned us that powder compressed inside an aluminium cup could eject molten metal when melted, presumably from trapped gas.

**Proposed fix to evaluate.** Use uniaxial die pressing (powder metallurgy) to turn the powder, alone or blended with aluminium powder, into a partly dense compact (a "semi-solid" pellet or slug under 20 mm in diameter), either as pressed (green) or after sintering, warm pressing, hot pressing or vacuum hot pressing, and melt that in the crucible instead of loose powder in a cup.

Please address:

1. **Why loose or lightly packed aluminium-alloy powder fails to melt into a bath** at 810-840 °C under argon: oxide shells (Al2O3, and MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel for Mg-bearing alloys), low thermal conductivity of a powder bed, entrapped gas, poor wetting, floating agglomerates. Does the Mg in AlSi10Mg plausibly explain why its powder failed while 4047 (no Mg) melted?
2. **Does uniaxial compaction fix it, and at what pressure and relative density?** Does particle deformation break the oxide films enough for metal-to-metal contact and coalescence on melting? Use evidence from remelting aluminium powder, chips or swarf (loose versus cold-compacted versus hot-compacted, metal yield or recovery), remelting PM green or sintered compacts, and aluminium foundry alloying tablets or compacts (Mn, Fe, Cr, Ti, Cu, Ni with aluminium powder, with and without flux): their dissolution times versus melt temperature, compact density and stirring. Also the dissolution of Si added as lump, powder or compact to aluminium melts.
3. **Safety and quality risks of melting a compact**: is the "ejects molten metal" warning justified, and under what conditions (closed porosity, hydrated oxide or moisture on the powder, die lubricants, a compact dropped into a melt versus heated up with the charge from cold)? How do these change from green to sintered to hot-pressed? Effects on oxygen and hydrogen in the melt, on oxide films and inclusions that could clog a 0.7 mm nozzle, and on contamination from lubricants or fluxes.
4. **Practical recipe if compaction is worthwhile**: pressure (MPa), target relative density, die-wall versus admixed lubricant, degassing or drying before pressing, vacuum pressing, sintering atmosphere and temperature, whether to blend with aluminium powder, compact size, where in the charge to put it, and how much extra superheat or hold time it needs. What press force does a 19 mm compact need at those pressures?
5. **How it compares with the alternatives** for 100-350 g induction melts aimed at a homogeneous target composition, low oxygen and no nozzle clogging: compacting the powder inside the cup with a vented sliding plug, a freestanding green compact, a sintered or hot-pressed compact, arc-melting a master alloy button first, buying commercial master alloys (for example Al-50Si, Al-20Si, Al-50Mg, Al-50Cu) or pre-alloyed powder, using a flux, or raising the melt temperature and hold time. Which would you recommend, and when would a pressed compact be the wrong choice?
6. **A quick test** that would tell us whether a compact melts in and mixes, before committing an atomizer run.

Please be explicit about which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium systems and which are extrapolated from other metals.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Simple and potentially energy efficient way for synthesis of Al/Al2O3 composites is described. Synthesis method is based on aluminum powder oxidation in water at 100-200 °C and following drying and calcination at 600 °C. Aluminum powder with average size of about 40 urn that is currently applied in additive manufacturing was used. Present work was devoted to the study of oxidation degree of aluminum and so the propagation depth and structure of Al2O3 shell in composite’s matrix. AI/Al2O3 composites were produced in different regimes with different maximum temperature and duration of the process of aluminium oxidation in water. Aluminum oxidation degree and aluminium content in obtained Al/Al2O3 were changed in the range from 5.5 % and 90.1 % to 21.3 % and 66.2 % respectively. The size of single crystals of Al2O3 in shell was changed from about 6 nm to 200 nm and the thickness of Al2O3 shell was changed from about 400 nm to 1000 nm by changing the regime for Al/Al2O3 composite production. Experimental results showed that Al2O3 shell was well clutched with aluminum core. Shell structure had cracks aroused by calcination process. Size distribution for obtained composites was very close for that of initial aluminum powder. All of these characteristics recommend the obtained Al/Al2O3 composites for additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Hybrid aluminum matrix composites (HAMCs) reinforced with graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) and secondary reinforcements have emerged as promising lightweight structural materials due to their superior strength, wear resistance, and multifunctional performance. This review critically evaluates recent developments in GNPs-reinforced HAMCs, categorizing them into carbide-assisted, oxide-assisted, carbonaceous, and emerging sustainable hybrid systems. The influence of processing routes including semi-solid stir casting (compocasting), ultrasonic-assisted stir casting (UASC), powder metallurgy (PM), friction stir processing (FSP), accumulative roll bonding (ARB), and laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) on reinforcement dispersion, interfacial bonding, and resultant properties (grain refinement, load-transfer mechanisms, etc.) is systematically discussed. Further, particular emphasis is placed on the role of the hybrid reinforcements in improving the mechanical and tribological performances of the HAMCs in reference to their processing techniques. Comparative analysis reveals that carbide-assisted systems provide the highest strengthening response, where Al/(GNPs+SiC) composites achieve tensile strengths up to 589 MPa through severe grain refinement, while GNPs+WC systems exhibit nearly 350% relative strength enhancement. Among oxide-assisted systems, L-PBF fabricated AA2024/(0.2GNPs+1ZrO2) (wt.%) composites attain a peak tensile strength of 624 MPa after T6 treatment due to the formation of a crack-free bimodal microstructure. Carbonaceous hybrids such as reduced graphene oxide (rGO)+CNTs systems demonstrate an excellent balance between strength (460 MPa) and ductility (31.6%) through interconnected carbon networks that suppress crack propagation. Tribologically, graphene-based tribo-films significantly reduce friction and wear, with GO+CNTs hybrids achieving a minimum coefficient of friction of 0.295, whereas GNPs+B4C and GNPs+waste-derived Al hybrid systems exhibit excellent wear resistance with wear rates as low as 1.9x10-3 mm3 m-1. The review further highlights key challenges including reinforcement agglomeration, porosity, and interfacial instability at higher GNPs loadings (>1–2 wt.%). Overall, the study provides a comparative and data-driven framework for designing next-generation HAMCs for aerospace, automotive, defense, and thermal-management applications.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Soft magnetic materials are critical to the performance, energy efficiency, and miniaturization of electric motors. While laminated soft magnetic materials have dominated the industry, the demand for soft magnetic composites (SMCs) is rapidly growing in applications requiring three-dimensional magnetic flux paths, reduced eddy current losses, and high-frequency operation. This study reports for the first time, in-situ friction stir forging (I-FSF), an innovative and single-step consolidation process for Fe-3.5Si soft magnetic powders. By leveraging pre-oxidized powders, the process generates oxide layers that enhance electrical resistivity. Unlike conventional sintering methods that require prolonged diffusion times, I-FSF promotes rapid densification and enables near-net-shape fabrication of dense SMC components with exceptional structural integrity in a single-step. The resulting components exhibit outstanding performance metrics, including tensile strength exceeding 650 MPa, saturation magnetization of 187 emu/g, and coercivity below 10 Oe, achieving the ideal balance between mechanical durability and magnetic efficiency. The proposed I-FSF process offers a simplified manufacturing route for producing advanced SMCs tailored for next generation electric motor applications, providing an alternative approach to magnetic material fabrication.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study investigates the influence of nano-sized reinforcements on aluminum matrix composites’ mechanical and tribological properties. Microstructural analysis revealed that introducing nanoparticles led to grain refinement, reducing the grain size from 129.7 μm to 41.3 μm with 2 wt.% TiO2 addition. Furthermore, ultrasonic-assisted squeeze casting of AA6061 composites reinforced with TiO2 and Al2O3 resulted in a 52% decrease in grain size, demonstrating nano-reinforcements’ effectiveness in refining the matrix structure. Despite these advantages, the high surface energy of nanoparticles causes agglomeration, which can undermine composite performance. However, ultrasonic-assisted stir casting reduced agglomeration by approximately 80% compared to conventional stir casting, and cold isostatic pressing improved dispersion uniformity by 27%. The incorporation of nano-reinforcements such as SiC, Al2O3, and TiC significantly enhanced the material properties, with hardness increasing by ~30% and ultimate tensile strength improving by ~80% compared to pure Al. The hardness of nano-reinforced composites substantially rose from 83 HV (pure Al) to 117 HV with 1.0 vol.% CNT reinforcement. Additionally, TiC-reinforced AA7075 composites improved hardness from 94.41 HB to 277.55 HB after 10 h of milling, indicating a nearly threefold increase. The wear resistance of Al-Si alloys was notably improved, with wear rates reduced by up to 52%, while the coefficient of friction decreased by 20–40% with the incorporation of graphene and CNT reinforcements. These findings highlight the potential of nano-reinforcements in significantly improving the mechanical and tribological performance of n-AMCs, making them suitable for high-performance applications in aerospace, automotive, and structural industries.
