Abstract:
Various foaming agents can be used to achieve foaming of the precursors obtained by using the powder metallurgy method. However, the thermal behavior of pure aluminum precursors with different foaming agents has been studied very little in recent times. For the production of aluminum foams with closed cells, 1 wt.% of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), titanium hydride (TiH2), heat-treated TiH2 and zirconium hydride (ZrH2) were used. The foaming capability of the compacted precursors was investigated at temperatures 700, 720 and 750 °C. CaCO3 and TiH2 showed the best foamability at all considered temperatures, while ZrH2 achieved relatively good foaming only at the highest temperature, 750 °C. Due to their low onset temperature of the decomposition compared to the melting point of the unalloyed aluminum, in hydride-based foaming agents the drainage occurred at the bottom part of the foam samples. Among the investigated foaming agents, precursors with heat-treated TiH2 had the worst foaming properties, while CaCO3 showed the best foamability without the occurrence of drainage.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The cleanliness of aluminium alloys has a decisive effect on their properties and performance. In this work, the melts of several Al-Mg-Si alloys (6xxx series) were refined using rotary flux injection (RFI) of the salt fluxes in the industrial environment. A typical charge consisted of 25 % to 30 % external scrap, 45 % to 50 % internal scrap, and 20 % to 30 % primary aluminium. During injection, the entire melt volume was mixed uniformly. The melt was filtered using a porous ring filtration apparatus. The fraction and type of non-metallic inclusions were determined using light and scanning electron microscopy. The contents of alkali and alkaline-earth metals were determined using optical emission spectroscopy. The reduction of alkali and alkaline earth metals and the fraction of non-metallic inclusions were used to evaluate the process efficiency and the flux selection for the regular production. An analysis of more than 100 industry charges confirmed that the flux selected after the experimental trials, consisting of a mixture of MgCl2, KCl, NaCl and CaF2, was effective in regular production.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this work, Al-11Fe, Al-7Fe-4Ni and Al-7Fe-4Cr (in wt. %) alloys were prepared by combination of casting and hot extrusion. Microstructures of as-cast alloys were composed of aluminium matrix with large and coarse intermetallics such as Al13Fe4, Al13Cr2 and Al5Cr. Subsequently, as-cast alloys were rapidly solidified by melt-spinning technique which led to the supersaturation of solid solution alloying elements. These rapidly solidified ribbons were milled and compacted by hot-extrusion method. Hot-extrusion caused that microstructures of all alloys were fine with uniform dispersed particles. Moreover, long-term thermal stability was tested at temperature 300 °C for as-cast and hot-extruded alloys and chromium was found to be the most suitable element for alloying to improve thermal stability.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Recently, “meltless” recycling techniques have been presented for the light metals category, targeting both energy and material savings by bypassing the final recycling step of remelting. In this context, the use of spark plasma sintering (SPS) is proposed in this paper as a novel solid-state recycling technique. The objective is two-fold: (I) to prove the technical feasibility of this approach; and (II) to characterize the recycled samples. Aluminum (Al) alloy scrap was selected to demonstrate the SPS effectiveness in producing fully-dense samples. For this purpose, Al alloy scrap in the form of machining chips was cold pre-compacted and sintered bellow the solidus temperature at 490 °C, under elevated pressure of 200 MPa. The dynamic scrap compaction, combined with electric current-based joule heating, achieved partial fracture of the stable surface oxides, desorption of the entrapped gases and activated the metallic surfaces, resulting in efficient solid-state chip welding eliminating residual porosity. The microhardness, the texture, the mechanical properties, the microstructure and the density of the recycled specimens have been investigated. An X-ray computed tomography (CT) analysis confirmed the density measurements, revealing a void-less bulk material with homogeneously distributed intermetallic compounds and oxides. The oxide content of the chips incorporated within the recycled material slightly increases its elastic properties. Finally, a thermal distribution simulation of the process in different segments illustrates the improved energy efficiency of this approach.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The demand for lightweight, high-performance, and multifunctional structures has driven rapid advances in multi-material joining technologies across aerospace, automotive, and electronics industries. Traditional joining methods often struggle with challenges such as thermal distortion, brittle intermetallic formation, and residual stresses when bonding dissimilar materials. This review critically examines three advanced additive manufacturing techniques—Ultrasonic Consolidation (UC), Cold Spray (CS), and Electron Beam Melting (EBM)—that offer promising solutions for multi-material fabrication. The mechanisms, material compatibility, microstructural evolution, and mechanical performance of joints produced by each process are systematically discussed. UC and CS, as solid-state processes, minimize thermal damage and oxidation, enabling strong joints between metals with dissimilar properties. EBM, operating in a high-vacuum environment, allows precise control over microstructure and enables the fabrication of complex, high-performance components. The novelty of this review lies in its integrative comparison of solid-state and fusion-based techniques, with a specific focus on their effectiveness in multi-material structural applications. It emphasizes interface behavior, residual stress development, and scalability challenges, while highlighting underexplored directions such as hybrid processing, interface engineering, tailored material feedstocks, and in-situ monitoring strategies. However, challenges such as bonding efficiency, residual stress management, and scalability remain. Future research directions are proposed, including process optimization, interface engineering, expanded material libraries, and integrated real-time monitoring to fully realize the potential of these emerging technologies for multi-material structural applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminium metal matrix composites (AMMCs) incorporate aluminium alloys reinforced with fibres (continuous/discontinuous), whiskers, or particulate. These materials were engineered as advanced solutions for demanding sectors including construction, aerospace, automotive, and marine. Micro- and nano-scale reinforcing particles typically enable attainment of exceptional combined properties, including reduced density with ultra-high strength, enhanced fatigue strength, superior creep resistance, high specific strength, and specific stiffness. Microstructural, mechanical, and tribological characterizations were performed, evaluating input parameters like reinforcement weight percentage, applied normal load, sliding speed, and sliding distance. Fabricated nanocomposites underwent tribometer testing to quantify abrasive and erosive wear behaviour. Multiple investigations employed the Taguchi technique with regression modelling. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) assessed the influence of varied test constraints. Applied load constituted the most significant factor affecting the physical/statistical attributes of nanocomposites. Sliding velocity critically governed the coefficient of friction (COF), becoming highly significant for minimizing COF and wear loss. In this review, the reinforcement homogeneity, fractural behaviour, and worn surface morphology of AMMCswere examined.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The escalating demands of pulsed power technology and high-energy-density capacitors necessitate dielectric ceramics with simultaneously enhanced breakdown reliability and microstructural homogeneity. Herein, Al2O3-MgAl2O4 composites were fabricated via a solid-state reaction using 80 wt% α-Al2O3 with kaolin/MgO mass ratios of 7:1, 4:1, and 1:1. XRD presents a dual-pathway spinel formation mechanism. SEM reveals 2–5 μm columnar spinel grains uniformly dispersed at grain boundaries. Porosity decreased from 4.29% to 2.69% while grain size increased from 3.35 to 5.64 μm as MgO content rose. Weibull analysis (n ≥ 10) showed that the 4:1 group achieved optimal dielectric reliability with a characteristic breakdown strength of 17.74 kV/mm and a Weibull modulus of 16.07, representing 8.76% and 20.93% improvements over the 7:1 (16.31 kV/mm, m = 24.58) and 1:1 (14.67 kV/mm, m = 15.37) groups, respectively. The 4:1 composition balanced grain boundary pinning (4.61 μm) and residual porosity (3.59%), maximizing interfacial charge scattering. Excess MgO (1:1) introduced residual Mg2+ into the glassy phase, inducing ionic conduction and premature breakdown. This study establishes a quantitative “microstructural composition–defect size distribution–dielectric breakdown” correlation, providing a theoretical foundation for microstructural optimization of low-cost alumina-based energy storage ceramics.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Aluminum and its alloys having lots of advantageous properties are among the most-used metallic materials. So, it is of immense importance to find suitable processes and methods leading to high-quality purified Al melt. In this regard, there are numerous challenges in achieving high purity Al melts, such as its propensity to react with air, oxygen, and water vapor, the presence of a variety of oxide, non-oxide, and solid particle inclusions that lead to the production of pores, cracks, pinholes, and dross, finally adversely influencing the overall quality of the product. The main methods of melt refining are fluxing, floatation, and filtration, but more sophisticated methods have also emerged. The best method for purification can be chosen based on the type of impurities and the desired level of purification. With the industrial development, the need to establish more cost-effective and simpler methods has increased, and in addition, methods should be considered for recycling large volumes of scarp Al parts that contain more impurities. Moreover, achieving high purity melt is also a vital issue for use in specific applications. The present article has been written to discuss the above issues and focus on the study of various methods of aluminum purification.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Aluminum recycling is pivotal for achieving carbon neutrality and advancing the circular economy, offering significant reductions in energy use and greenhouse gas emissions compared to primary production. This review synthesizes global advances from 2020 to 2025 in scrap collection, sorting, remelting, and alloy recovery, with a focus on technological progress, sustainability metrics, and policy integration. Secondary aluminum already supplies over one-third of global demand and could surpass 50 % by 2030 with stronger segregation systems and extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes. Innovations such as high-shear degassing, solid-state chip recycling, and chloride-free refining have improved melt quality and reduced salt-slag waste. At the same time, life-cycle assessments indicate up to 95% lower emissions compared to virgin aluminum. Persistent barriers remain—namely alloy contamination, inconsistent scrap classification, and limited traceability in informal collection networks. Regional policy experiences demonstrate that harmonized standards, mandatory recycled-content targets, and digital traceability accelerate market adaptation, whereas developing economies still face fragmented logistics and weak governance. Future directions include integrating real-time life-cycle assessment, artificial intelligence-based scrap sorting, and international alloy standards, enabling over 80% recycled content. Overall, aluminum recycling emerges as a technologically mature, economically competitive, and environmentally decisive route for decarbonizing metallurgical production and supporting the global energy transition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Scrap-based melting is essential to the decarbonization of foundry production, but scrap selection is still often treated as a purchasing decision rather than as an integrated metallurgical design problem. This structured critical narrative review evaluated an audited corpus of 105 publications published from 2020 to August 2026. Evidence coding identified 40 aluminum-focused studies, 25 steel-focused studies, 7 cast-iron studies, 7 copper-alloy studies, 1 nickel-base study, and 25 cross-cutting contributions. Only 15 studies were industrial or pilot demonstrations, whereas 55 were laboratory studies and 35 were models, reviews, or contextual analyses. Nominal chemistry alone was consistently insufficient to determine scrap fitness: origin, size distribution, bulk density, coatings, oxide load, entrained contaminants, sampling uncertainty, and furnace-specific response jointly controlled metallic yield, energy demand, melt cleanliness, residual-element accumulation, emissions, and off-specification risk. The review proposes a normalized mass-balance formulation, probabilistic chemistry constraints, a cost-per-tonne-of-conforming-metal objective, and a four-gate scrap-to-alloy framework.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt identifies the native oxide shell on aluminium powder as the principal obstacle to consolidation. The shell is tenacious and inhibits diffusion between neighbouring aluminium particles, preventing the metal-to-metal contact needed for bonding. Aluminium oxide is also thermodynamically very stable; reducing it requires an extremely low oxygen partial pressure (about 10^-43 Pa), so simply heating loose powder in an aluminium melt does not readily eliminate the barrier. Mechanical deformation during ordinary powder compaction can crack or disrupt the oxide only partially and is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering. Other possible disruption mechanisms include cracking during heating, liquid penetration through discontinuities, and chemical reaction with magnesium. Mg can react with the aluminium oxide shell to form MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel, thereby creating discontinuities or reducing the oxide and allowing a liquid phase to penetrate to the underlying aluminium. This improves wetting, particle bonding, and sinterability. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative Mg-content dependence or explicitly compare the stability of Al2O3, MgO, and MgAl2O4 as Mg concentration changes. It does, however, indicate that an effective Mg level depends on oxide volume; in an Al-Sn example, 0.15% Mg was reported as optimal, while insufficient Mg left poor sintering and liquid exudation.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 45-49'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt indicates that aluminium powder particles are covered by a persistent oxide layer, and that merely compacting the powder—or exposing it to liquid—does not necessarily produce effective particle bonding or consolidation. The oxide shell acts as a barrier at particle contacts, preventing intimate aluminium-to-aluminium contact, limiting wetting and diffusion, and thereby hindering melting, liquid spreading, and coalescence. In aluminium–magnesium systems, Mg reacts with alumina and can transform the interfacial oxide into MgO and/or MgAl2O4 spinel. These phases are explicitly observed at SPS-sintered Al–Mg interfaces. Mg can therefore modify oxide-shell chemistry and, at an appropriate concentration, promote oxide disruption or facilitate rupture during processing; the excerpt specifically attributes improved sintering and high density to Mg-assisted oxide disruption. However, oxide rupture is not automatically sufficient: the Al–Sn system showed poor sintering without Mg despite mechanical compaction. The text also reports an optimum Mg concentration associated with improved strength, ductility, and particle bonding, implying that Mg content strongly affects shell stability and interfacial bonding. Excessive or non-optimal Mg effects are not quantified in this excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000002

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 199-204'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt identifies the persistent oxide film surrounding aluminium powder particles as the principal obstacle to consolidation. Because the tenacious oxide shell prevents effective sintering and limits metal-to-metal contact, particles do not readily bond or coalesce even when compacted. Conventional sintering is generally insufficient to disrupt this film; liquid-phase sintering is preferred because a liquid can penetrate and wet the particle surfaces once the oxide barrier is chemically weakened. Magnesium acts as a sintering aid by reducing Al2O3 and forming MgO, whose lower free energy enables disruption of the alumina barrier and improves liquid wetting. The text therefore supports the view that oxide shells act as physical and chemical barriers to melting-related contact, wetting, and coalescence. It also emphasizes that pressure, plastic deformation, and localized Joule heating can break down oxide films and increase metal-to-metal interfaces. However, this excerpt does not specifically describe loose powder added directly to an aluminium melt, nor does it detail MgAl2O4 spinel formation or quantify how Mg concentration affects shell stability. Its evidence is strongest for Al2O3 persistence, Mg-assisted oxide reduction, and mechanically assisted shell disruption during SPS and forging.


---

## pqac-00000003

From text 'ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 53-57'.

AH Ibrahim. Effect of material and processing parameters on the morphology of aluminium foams produced by the pm route. Unknown journal, 2005.

The excerpt indicates that loose aluminium powder does not readily melt into a continuous mass because each air-atomized particle is covered by a persistent oxide film. Air-atomized aluminium powder typically has an oxide layer about 50–150 Å thick; the oxide is initially amorphous and hydrous (Al2O3·3H2O), and can crystallize to γ-Al2O3 during heating above 350°C. During atomization, oxide forms on droplet surfaces, changes their surface energy, inhibits spheroidization, and oxide fragments may become trapped inside particles. Most importantly for consolidation, oxide-covered surfaces do not weld together effectively: the oxide prevents direct metal-to-metal contact and can leave micropores where particle surfaces fail to bond. Thus, the oxide shell acts as a diffusion/contact barrier to melting, wetting, coalescence, and pore elimination. The excerpt does not discuss MgO, MgAl2O4 spinel, or how magnesium concentration changes oxide-shell stability. Therefore, it supports the general role of Al2O3 as a barrier but provides no direct evidence for Mg-dependent shell stabilization or transformation; those aspects require another source.


---

## pqac-00000004

From text 'ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 32-36'.

AH Ibrahim. Effect of material and processing parameters on the morphology of aluminium foams produced by the pm route. Unknown journal, 2005.

The excerpt explains that aluminium powder particles are covered by thin Al2O3 films, approximately 50–150 Å thick, together with trapped oxides formed during atomization. These oxide layers do not simply disappear during heating; instead, they become incorporated into a branched, crumpled oxide-network structure. The network fragments can be captured between particles and within cell walls, where they act as mechanical barriers. This barrier effect helps prevent liquid-metal drainage and supports foam stability, but it also indicates why oxide-covered aluminium particles can resist complete liquid consolidation and coalescence: the oxide remains as an interparticle skeleton that impedes direct metal-to-metal contact and flow. The excerpt further reports that increasing powder oxygen content above 0.40 wt.% eliminates the thick drainage zone at the bottom of the foam, demonstrating the strong effect of oxide content on liquid-metal movement. However, the provided passage does not specifically discuss MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel, nor does it explain how Mg concentration changes oxide-shell stability on aluminium powder. Therefore, it supports the general role of oxide shells as barriers and stabilizers, but additional source material is needed for the Mg-dependent oxide chemistry and the detailed failure of loose powder to melt and consolidate in an aluminium melt.


---

## pqac-00000005

From text 'kraus2016consolidationofaerospace pages 89-93'.

N Kraus. Consolidation of aerospace grade aluminum 7055 powder via pm technologies. Unknown journal, 2016.

The excerpt is a bibliography rather than a discussion of the melting and consolidation mechanism, so it does not directly explain why loose aluminium alloy powder fails to melt or coalesce in an aluminium melt. It does, however, identify several directly relevant studies. The cited works on “Surface Oxides in P/M Aluminum Alloys,” the “sintering of aluminium,” and oxide-film behavior at particle interfaces indicate that persistent surface oxide layers are central to aluminium-powder consolidation. Such shells can prevent liquid aluminium from directly wetting and bonding adjacent particles, mechanically constrain particle rearrangement, and preserve separate powder surfaces even when the aluminium core is molten. The references specifically addressing magnesium—“Effects of magnesium, tin and nitrogen on the sintering response of aluminum powder” and “Reduction of Surface Oxide Films in Al–Mg Alloy Powders”—suggest that Mg changes oxide-film chemistry and stability. In aluminium alloys, Mg can react with the native Al2O3 film and form MgO and MgAl2O4 spinel; these oxides may remain refractory and act as barriers to wetting, rupture, and coalescence. The excerpt itself does not state the direction or quantitative dependence of shell stability on Mg content, nor does it explicitly discuss Al2O3/MgO/spinel formation. Those details would need to be obtained from the cited full articles.


---

## pqac-00000006

From text 'ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 25-29'.

AH Ibrahim. Effect of material and processing parameters on the morphology of aluminium foams produced by the pm route. Unknown journal, 2005.

The excerpt does not directly discuss why loose aluminium alloy powder fails to melt and consolidate in an aluminium melt, nor does it specifically compare Al2O3, MgO, and MgAl2O4 spinel or quantify the effect of magnesium content on oxide-shell stability. It does, however, identify oxide networks and oxide fragments as important structural features of powder-metallurgical aluminium foams. Careful precursor manufacture is required because defects, residual porosity, and nonuniform distributions produce an inhomogeneous structure. During early foaming, hydrogen pressure can form cracks in the still-solid compact; these cracks fragment the oxide network and can cause loss of gas. The excerpt also states that solid oxide particles in molten metal can destabilize cell walls and promote rupture. In PM foam, the particles involved in stabilization are described as crumbled oxide-network fragments. Thus, the passage supports the relevance of persistent oxide-derived barriers or particles to powder consolidation and melt stability, but it does not provide the requested mechanistic detail about oxide-shell resistance to melting/coalescence or how increasing Mg changes shell composition and stability.

Abstract:

 In this work, the effective thermal conductivity of sintered powder materials is studied. The extensive literature related to the proposed models about this property in all kind of porous materials is reviewed, and a new equation is proposed as a function of the fully dense material conductivity, the porosity of the material and the tap porosity of the starting powder. This equation covers the porosity range of powder aggregates from the tap porosity to zero porosity, and also applies to sintered powders. The proposed equation has been experimentally validated by fitting to experimental data of metallic sintered powder materials measured at room temperature, resulting very good agreements. Also, alternative models proposed by other authors have been fitted to the same experimental data to check the relative goodness of the proposed model. The results allow to conclude that a percolation model can describe the behaviour of the effective thermal conductivity of sintered powder materials with low and medium porosity levels.

Abstract:
Metamaterials are defined as artificially designed micro-architectures with unusual physical properties, including optical, electromagnetic, mechanical, and thermal characteristics. This study investigates the compressive mechanical and heat transfer properties of AlSi10Mg gradient metamaterials fabricated by Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). The morphology of the AlSi10Mg metamaterials was examined using an ultrahigh-resolution microscope. Quasi-static uniaxial compression tests were conducted at room temperature, with deformation behavior captured through camera recordings. The findings indicate that the proposed gradient metamaterial exhibits superior compressive strength properties and energy absorption capacity. The Gradient-SplitP structure demonstrated better compressive performance compared to other strut-based structures, including Gradient-Gyroid and Gradient-Lidinoid structures. With an apparent density of 0.796, the Gradient-SplitP structure exhibited an outstanding energy absorption capacity, reaching an impressive 23.57 MJ/m3. In addition, heat conductivity tests were performed to assess the thermal resistance of these structures with different cell configurations. The gradient metamaterials exhibited higher thermal resistance and lower thermal conductivity. Consequently, the designed gradient metamaterials can be considered valuable in various applications, such as thermal management, load-bearing, and energy absorption components.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Among different promising solutions, coupling closed-cell aluminium foam composite panels prepared by a powder metallurgical method with pore walls interconnected by microcracks, with low thermal conductivity phase change materials (PCMs), is one of the effective ways of increasing thermal conductivity for better performance of thermal storage systems in buildings. The internal structure of the foam formation, related to the porosity which decides the heat transfer rate, plays a significant role in the thermal energy storage performance. The dependence of the heat transfer characteristics on the internal foam structure is studied numerically in this work. The foamable precursor of 99.7% pure aluminium powder mixed with 0.15 wt.% of foaming agent, TiH2 powder, was prepared by compacting, and extruded to a volume of 20 × 40 × 5 mm. Two aluminium foam samples of 40 × 40 × 5 mm were examined with apparent densities of 0.7415 g/cm3 and 1.62375 g/cm3. The internal porous structure of the aluminium foam samples was modelled using X-ray tomography slices through image processing techniques for finite element analysis. The obtained numerical results for the heat transfer rate and effective thermal conductivity of the developed surrogate models revealed the influence of porosity, struts, and the presence of pore walls in determining the heat flow in the internal structure of the foam. Additionally, it was found that the pore size and its distribution determine the uniform heat flow rate in the entire foamed structure. The numerical data were then validated against the analytical predictions of thermal conductivity based on various correlations. It has been found that the simplified models of Bruggemann and Russell and the parallel–series model can predict the excellent effective thermal conductivity results of the foam throughout the porosity range. The optimal internal foam structure was studied to explore the possibilities of using aluminium foam for PCM-based thermal storage applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:

Purpose
AlSi10Mg alloy is commonly used in laser powder bed fusion due to its printability, relatively high thermal conductivity, low density and good mechanical properties. However, the thermal conductivity of as-built materials as a function of processing (energy density, laser power, laser scanning speed, support structure) and build orientation, are not well explored in the literature. This study aims to elucidate the relationship between processing, microstructure, and thermal conductivity.


Design/methodology/approach
The thermal conductivity of laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) AlSi10Mg samples are investigated by the flash diffusivity and frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) techniques. Thermal conductivities are linked to the microstructure of L-PBF AlSi10Mg, which changes with processing conditions. The through-plane exceeded the in-plane thermal conductivity for all energy densities. A co-located thermal conductivity map by frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) and crystallographic grain orientation map by electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) was used to investigate the effect of microstructure on thermal conductivity.


Findings
The highest through-plane thermal conductivity (136 ± 2 W/m-K) was achieved at 59 J/mm3 and exceeded the values reported previously. The in-plane thermal conductivity peaked at 117 ± 2 W/m-K at 50 J/mm3. The trend of thermal conductivity reducing with energy density at similar porosity was primarily due to the reduced grain size producing more Al-Si interfaces that pose thermal resistance. At these interfaces, thermal energy must convert from electrons in the aluminum to phonons in the silicon. The co-located thermal conductivity and crystallographic grain orientation maps confirmed that larger colonies of columnar grains have higher thermal conductivity compared to smaller columnar grains.


Practical implications
The thermal properties of AlSi10Mg are crucial to heat transfer applications including additively manufactured heatsinks, cold plates, vapor chambers, heat pipes, enclosures and heat exchangers. Additionally, thermal-based nondestructive testing methods require these properties for applications such as defect detection and simulation of L-PBF processes. Industrial standards for L-PBF processes and components can use the data for thermal applications.


Originality/value
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this paper is the first to make coupled thermal conductivity maps that were matched to microstructure for L-PBF AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy. This was achieved by a unique in-house thermal conductivity mapping setup and relating the data to local SEM EBSD maps. This provides the first conclusive proof that larger grain sizes can achieve higher thermal conductivity for this processing method and material system. This study also shows that control of the solidification can result in higher thermal conductivity. It was also the first to find that the build substrate (with or without support) has a large effect on thermal conductivity.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'montes2025porosityeffecton pages 4-6'.

J. M. Montes, F. G. Cuevas, J. Cintas, and F. Ternero. Porosity effect on the thermal conductivity of sintered powder materials. Applied Physics A, Jan 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00339-025-08254-y, doi:10.1007/s00339-025-08254-y. This article has 19 citations.

The excerpt explains that thermal conductivity in porous powder materials is controlled primarily by the amount of solid material and the quality or area of interparticle contacts. In a loose aluminium powder bed, particles have only small contact areas and much of the volume is air-filled, so heat conduction through the solid network is strongly reduced; the air contribution is also very small compared with metallic conduction. The proposed model represents effective thermal conductivity as decreasing with normalized porosity, from the conductivity of fully dense material (κ0) toward the conductivity of air (κair) as porosity approaches its maximum. At 20 °C, air has a thermal conductivity of only 0.026 W·m−1·K−1, while aluminium’s conductivity is much higher. Compaction improves thermal conductivity by reducing porosity and increasing the solid fraction and interparticle contact area, thereby creating better continuous pathways for heat flow. At low residual porosity, the model predicts approximately linear improvement with decreasing porosity. The excerpt does not provide a specific numerical comparison between loose and solid aluminium powder beds, but it supplies the physical mechanism and model describing why compaction raises conductivity.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'montes2025porosityeffecton pages 6-7'.

J. M. Montes, F. G. Cuevas, J. Cintas, and F. Ternero. Porosity effect on the thermal conductivity of sintered powder materials. Applied Physics A, Jan 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00339-025-08254-y, doi:10.1007/s00339-025-08254-y. This article has 19 citations.

The excerpt does not provide a direct measured thermal-conductivity value for a loose aluminium powder bed, so it cannot establish a numerical loose-bed-to-solid-aluminium comparison from these pages alone. It does provide the relevant aluminium reference and compaction conditions. AS61 aluminium powder has an absolute density of 2.70 g/cm³ and a tap porosity of 0.45, indicating substantial void space in the loose/tapped powder state. Compacts were made by uniaxial cold pressing, with pressure varied to produce different porosities; the maximum pressure used was 1400 MPa, producing the lowest porosity. The aluminium compacts covered a final porosity range of 0.01–0.32. Consequently, the effective thermal conductivity of a porous powder bed is expected to be lower than that of a continuous solid, with the extent depending on porosity, apparent density, particle arrangement, gas pressure, and particle-to-particle contact. This shifts heat transfer toward conduction through the solid particle network and generally improves the bed’s effective thermal conductivity. The excerpt also notes that particle size and contact effects can be competing factors: finer particles may fill pores and create more contact area, but increased particle contacts can introduce thermal contact resistance. Mechanical alloying (MA) of powders represents the first processing step in the production of oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) alloys. MA is a time and energy-consuming process also in the production of Fe-10Al-4Cr-4Y2O3 creep and oxidation-resistant ODS nanocomposite, denoted as the FeAlOY, and it deserves to be optimized. MA is performed at two different temperatures at different times. Thus, the conditions of MA correspond to sufficient dissolution and homogenization of Y2O3 and can be considered the optimal ones.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing of lightweight metallic alloys, particularly aluminum- and titanium-based systems, has emerged as a transformative approach for producing high-performance components with unprecedented design freedom. Among available technologies, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) offers superior geometrical resolution and microstructural control; however, the successful processing of lightweight alloys remains constrained by fundamental challenges related to printability, defect formation, and microstructural heterogeneity. This review critically examines the process–structure–property relationships governing L-PBF fabrication of aluminum and titanium alloys, with a specific focus on the mechanisms of defect generation and their implications for mechanical performance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>First, the unique thermophysical characteristics of lightweight alloys—including high reflectivity, oxidation tendency, and rapid solidification kinetics—are analyzed in the context of melt pool dynamics and thermal gradients. Second, alloy-specific microstructural evolution is discussed, highlighting the formation of cellular structures in Al–Si systems and martensitic transformations in Ti–6Al–4 V, alongside their dependence on process parameters. Third, the dominant defect mechanisms, including lack-of-fusion porosity, keyhole-induced voids, hydrogen gas porosity, and hot cracking, are systematically compared between aluminum and titanium alloys, establishing clear cause–effect relationships between processing conditions and structural integrity.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Building upon these insights, the review integrates recent advances in computational modeling approaches—such as CALPHAD, phase-field simulations, and machine learning—to demonstrate how predictive frameworks can guide alloy design and process optimization. A cross-material comparison is further developed to identify critical differences and shared limitations in printability and performance. Finally, a unified design strategy is proposed, linking process control, alloy chemistry, and defect mitigation to enable the development of next-generation lightweight materials tailored for additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This work provides a focused and analytical perspective that bridges fundamental mechanisms with practical design strategies, offering a roadmap for advancing lightweight alloy applications in aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors.</jats:p>

The excerpt does not report measured thermal-conductivity values for a loose aluminium powder bed. It gives the AS61 aluminium powder’s tap porosity as ΘM = 0.45 and lists a fitted parameter κ0 = 231.71 W/(m·K), obtained from fitting thermal-conductivity data for sintered compacts—not from a loose powder-bed measurement. The study’s aluminium compacts covered a final porosity range of 0.01–0.32, so this excerpt does not provide a direct value at the loose-bed condition (approximately the tap porosity). For comparison, the excerpt states that the literature thermal conductivity of fully dense pure aluminium is 238 W/(m·K). Thus, based solely on the supplied text, a quantitative reduction of loose-bed effective conductivity relative to solid aluminium cannot be calculated. The available κ0 value is only about 6.29 W/(m·K), or approximately 2.64%, below 238 W/(m·K), but it should not be interpreted as the loose powder-bed conductivity.

Thermal De-coating Pre-treatment for Loose or Compacted Aluminum Scrap and Consequences for Salt-Flux Recycling Valid Text Names: 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 1-3', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 3-4', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 4-6', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 6-8', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 8-10', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 10-11', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 11-12', 'vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 12-13' BibTex: @article{vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment, author = "Vallejo-Olivares, Alicia and Høgåsen, Solveig and Kvithyld, Anne and Tranell, Gabriella", title = "Thermal De-coating Pre-treatment for Loose or Compacted Aluminum Scrap and Consequences for Salt-Flux Recycling", year = "2022", journal = "Journal of Sustainable Metallurgy", volume = "8", pages = "1485-1497", month = "Oct", doi = "10.1007/s40831-022-00612-x", url = "https://doi.org/10.1007/s40831-022-00612-x", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "4", issn = "2199-3823" } Abstract: In aluminum recycling, thermal de-coating pre-treatments remove moisture and organic contamination before re-melting. If the scrap is compacted into bales or briquettes before the thermal treatment and re-melting processes, less surface area is exposed to oxidation in contact with air. However, compaction may also limit the efficiency of the de-coating process. In this study, coated sheets of aluminum were thermally de-coated at varied temperatures and durations. Observations of changes in coating thickness, mass, color, and composition revealed a maximum de-coating efficiency of close to 75% wt due to remaining oxide residues. The relationship between de-coating and compaction was investigated by thermally treating loose shreddings (chips) and briquettes of various densities. The briquettes were compacted by three methods: uniaxial, moderate-pressure torsion (MPT), and MPT at 450 °C (Hot MPT); and the de-coating efficiency was calculated from the mass loss. Subsequently, the samples were re-melted under salt-flux and compared with another set of samples which were re-melted without thermal pre-treatment. The results showed that thermal de-coating significantly promotes the coalescence of loose chips and briquettes compacted uniaxially, up to similar coalescences than initially uncoated aluminum samples. Thermally treating the MPT briquettes, which were more densely compacted, led to less de-coating, and subsequently lower coalescences. The analysis of re-melted material revealed that the coating residues did not significantly affect the composition, while the compaction prevented Mg loss for the uncoated materials. A solution is de-coating the scrap via a thermal pre-treatment to burn-off the organics before re-melting. Due to logistic benefits, the scrap is often pressed into bales. This study evaluates the influence of compaction on the de-coating efficiency and off-gas emissions, and its consequences for dross formation and recycling metal yield. Loose chips and two types of briquettes, one loosely compacted by uniaxial pressure and the other compacted by moderated-pressure-torsion to higher densities, were heated to 550 °C while analysing the off-gas emissions using FTIR. The briquettes were subsequently re-melted into a molten heel. Re-melting coated scrap multiplied the % wt of dross by a factor of 2 or 3, depending on the compaction pre-treatment, compared to re-melting uncoated aluminium. The densest briquettes emitted less than half the CO2 and CO gases during de-coating and formed significantly more dross. Compaction to the lower densities showed no tangible effects. The effect of de-coating compacted materials or not was small (± 2% wt dross), which was attributed to carbonaceous residues remaining after the thermal treatment. In conclusion, high compactions by torsion limit the de-coating reactions, which depend on factors such as temperature and gas transport. A complete removal of the organic residues is critical for a more sustainable recycling with less dross generated. ## pqac-00000018

From text 'baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20'.

Petr Baron, Jozef Mikita, and Vladimír Simkulet. Characterization of cold-pressed aluminum briquettes and their behavior during remelting for application in steel deoxidation. Unknown journal, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1, doi:10.20944/preprints202604.0191.v1.

The excerpt reports remelting performance for compacted aluminium briquettes, particularly Sample B. Its post-remelting density was 2.388 g·cm⁻³, with a dross fraction of 2.25%, relative melting loss of 3.55%, and metallurgical yield of 94.2%. The authors place this result within the expected 90–96% yield range for briquettes with densities around 2.15–2.40 g·cm⁻³, and identify 2.20–2.40 g·cm⁻³ as an optimal density range for steel deoxidation. Higher density and effective compaction improve the likelihood that briquettes fragment and submerge appropriately, while reducing mechanical voids; however, oxidation of chip surfaces still produces dross and metal loss. The excerpt does not provide a direct numerical yield or recovery comparison between briquetted/compacted chips and loose chips. It does indicate that loose or partially compacted feedstocks retain more entrapped gas, while residual oils and cutting emulsions decompose during heating, increasing gas porosity, metal burn-off, and lowering yield. The discussion therefore links remelting losses to briquette density, oxide-covered chip surface area, oil contamination, and pressing conditions. The authors recommend pretreatment and pressing sufficient to achieve densities above 2.35 g·cm⁻³.

The excerpt directly addresses the steam-explosion hazard when water or moisture is trapped within or enclosed by molten aluminum. In cited aluminum–water experiments, violent explosions required liquid water to become enclosed by a compact mass of aluminum and an aluminum temperature high enough to cause rapid, essentially explosive water vaporization, followed by rapid oxidation of the newly formed metal particles. Thus, wet, porous, or otherwise gas- or moisture-containing aluminum added to molten aluminum could create a sudden steam-generation and molten-metal dispersal event if the moisture is confined and heat transfer is rapid. The severity depends on the quantity of simultaneously reacting metal, the specific surface area of particles, metal temperature, water depth, stream geometry, and whether the metal forms a compact mass. Conditions that cool or disperse the aluminum reduce the likelihood of the described violent mechanism, while high temperature and confinement promote it. The passage does not specifically discuss hydrogen evolution, hydrated oxide decomposition, trapped non-water gas expansion, or oxide hydration during remelting, although it notes uncertainty about participating reactions and identifies rapid oxidation as part of the explosion sequence. Abstract:
Selected laser melting (SLM) is a representative process of powder-bed type 3D printing technology that is used to manipulate metals and it generally results in various structural properties according to the process conditions. In this study, a thermal conductivity test was conducted on AlSi10Mg specimens that were manufactured using the SLM process to investigate the influence of various process conditions on the thermophysical characteristics and cellular microstructure of the samples. The building direction of the specimen, laser scan speed, and hatch spacing were considered as process variables, and the thermal conductivity was analyzed for each process variable. In the test results, as the polar angle of the specimen increased from 0° to 90°, the thermal conductivity increased. Furthermore, the thermal conductivity gradually decreased as the scan speed and hatch spacing increased. The differences in thermal characteristics are discussed in connection with the microstructure of the cells constituting the melt pool. The solidified melt pool that formed by the laser beam is composed of cells consisting of an Al matrix and a surrounding Si-rich area. The differences in thermal conductivity of the overall specimens are explained based on the variations in thermal conductivity and cell shape and size for each chemical component.

Abstract:
Ce projet a ete entrepris pour etudier les interactions entre les particules d'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions sous des conditions d'ecoulement de l'aluminium liquide. Le but du projet etait de developper une methode d'essai qui permet de simuler les conditions similaires a celles dans le procede de filtration d'aluminium et d'evaluer les interactions qui ont lieu entre les differents types d'echantillons d'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions. Cette methode d'essai avait pour but de determiner commenles differents types d'alumine se comportent durant le procede de filtration.
 
Les interactions chimiques entre l'alumine, les alliages d'aluminium et ses inclusions ont ete etudiees dans des conditions d'ecoulement statiques et dynamique. Afin d'etudier ces interactions dans des conditions d'ecoulement dynamique, la connaissance du champ de vitesse au voisinage des particules d'alumine est necessaire. Dans ce projet, deux systemes experimentaux uniques qui peuvent simuler l'ecoulement dans le lit du filtre industriel ont ete concus et construits. Un modele mathematique a ete developpe pour predire le champ d'ecoulement autour des particules dans le systeme experimental. Le modele mathematique a ete valide en comparant les predictions avec les resultats d'un modele physique dans lequel l'eau etait utilisee comme fluide. Ensuite, le modele mathematique a ete utilise pour effectuer des etudes parametriques afin de determiner les parametres de design et d'operation pour le systeme experimental actuel dans lequel les tests ont ete faits. Cela a permis de generer un champ d'ecoulement similaire a celui du filtre industriel.
 
Des experiences avec divers alliages d'aluminium-magnesium liquide (0, 2, 5 et 7% Mg, en poids) ont ete realisees pour des differents temps de residence (de 6 heures a 168 heures) en utilisant les systemes experimentaux decrits ci-hauts. Les effets de la vitesse de l'alliage d'aluminium liquide, de la temperature du liquide, des proprietes physiques (porosite apparente, la rugosite de la surface, etc.) et chimiques (teneur en impuretes telles que Na2O, SiO2, etc.) sur le degre des reactions interfaciales entre l'alliage d'aluminium et l'alumine ont ete determines.
 
Les echantillons obtenus des experiences aluminium-alumina ont ete analyses a l'aide du microscope optique, du microscope electronique a balayage - la spectroscopie aux rayons X a dispersion d'energie (MEB-EDX), du microprobe MEB, et de la diffraction des rayons X (DRX). Les resultats montrent que les reactions chimiques entre l'alpha-alumine pure a haute densite et les alliages Mg-Al liquides ne sont pas rapide; mais, la presence des impuretes (telle que Na2O en tant que phase de beta-alumine) et la structure poreuse de l'alumine augmentent l'etendue des reactions significativement. La phase riche en Na2O (beta-alumine) qui se trouve dans toutes les alumines commerciales semble etre l'un des facteurs les plus importants pour les reactions spontanees avec la vapeur de magnesium, meme au temps de residence le plus court. Mg-spinelle a ete trouve comme le produit de reaction le plus important. L'analyse thermodynamique indique la meme tendance.

This project was undertaken to study the interactions between alumina particles, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions under liquid aluminum flow conditions. The objective was to develop a test method which can simulate the conditions similar to those in the aluminum filtration process and to evaluate the interactions taking place between various types of alumina samples, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions. With this test method, it was aimed to determine how various alumina types behave under flow conditions during the filtration process.
 
Chemical interactions between alumina, aluminum alloys, and its inclusions were investigated under both static and dynamic flow conditions. In order to study these interactions under dynamic flow conditions, a knowledge of the velocity field in the vicinity of the alumina particles is necessary. In this project, two unique experimental systems which can simulate the flow condition of the industrial bed were designed and built. A mathematical model was also developed to predict the flow field around the particles in the experimental system. The mathematical model was validated by comparing the predictions with the results from a physical model in which water was used as the fluid. The mathematical model was then used to conduct parametric studies to determine the design and operational parameters for the actual experimental system in which the tests were carried out. This allowed the generation of a flow field similar to that of the industrial filter.
 
The experiments with various liquid Mg-Al alloys (0, 2, 5, and 7 wt% Mg) were conducted for different residence times (from 6 hours to 168 hours) using the above experimental systems. The effects of the liquid aluminum alloy velocity, the temperature of the melt, the physical (apparent porosity, surface roughness, etc.) and chemical (impurity content such as Na2O, SiO2 etc.) properties of alumina samples on the extent of aluminum alloy/alumina interfacial reactions were determined.
 
The samples obtained from aluminum-alumina experiments were analyzed by using the optical microscope, the scanning electron microscope - energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX), the micro probe SEM, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results indicate that the chemical reactions between high density pure alpha-alumina and molten Mg-Al alloys are not fast; however, the presence of impurities (such as Na20 as beta alumina phase) and the porous structure in alumina increase the extent of reactions significantly. Na2O rich phase (beta alumina) found in all commercial alumina grades seems to be one of the most important contributors for the spontaneous reactions of Mg vapor with alumina, even at the shortest residence time. The major reaction product was found to be Mg-spinel. The thermodynamic analysis indicated the same tendency.

## pqac-00000032

V. Yu. Bazhin, S. A. Savchenkov, and Ya. I. Kosov. Specificity of the titanium-powder alloying tablets usage in aluminium alloys. ArXiv, pages 52-56, Dec 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11, doi:10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt reports that titanium alloying tablets or briquettes dissolve effectively in aluminium melt, with titanium assimilation to 0.20% taking no more than 40 minutes for specimens from different suppliers. The fastest dissolution was 28 minutes for a briquette containing molasses. Initial sampling after 5–7 minutes showed only a small titanium increase because transfer from the tablet surface was slow. After briquette breakup, titanium content increased rapidly. Tablet porosity is identified as a key factor: sufficient interconnected porosity allows molten aluminium to penetrate the compact and interact actively with titanium particles until complete dissolution. This implies that overconsolidated or excessively dense briquettes can hinder melt penetration and slow dissolution, although the excerpt does not provide a quantified density–dissolution relationship. Stirring, or using the alloying element in dispersed form, is recommended to accelerate melt saturation. Dissolution also occurs under free or forced convection, with isothermal holding time and selected melt temperature affecting the process, but no specific temperature values are given here. Molasses improves flux adhesion to titanium powder and strengthens the tablets during pressing; the figure compares porosity backgrounds with and without molasses. Listed tablet densities range approximately from 3.28 to 4.12 g/cm³, alongside mechanical strength ratings, but these data are not directly correlated with dissolution time.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 2-4'.

V. Yu. Bazhin, S. A. Savchenkov, and Ya. I. Kosov. Specificity of the titanium-powder alloying tablets usage in aluminium alloys. ArXiv, pages 52-56, Dec 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11, doi:10.17580/nfm.2016.12.11. This article has 18 citations.

The excerpt identifies compact density and porosity as major controls on titanium alloying-tablet dissolution in aluminium melt. The recommended tablet density is 2.5–5.0 g/cm3, obtained at an optimum compaction pressure of 250–300 kg/cm2 (25.5–29.8 MPa). Excessive pressure, 350–500 kg/cm2, can fracture titanium powder particles internally. During melting, aluminium can penetrate these voids, allowing flux–metal interaction and oxide formation, which ultimately becomes slag. Overconsolidated briquettes have insufficient porosity, so the moving aluminium melt cannot infiltrate them fully; they may form a barrier oxide layer and dissolve slowly, with a reported dissolution rate of 35–40 minutes. Conversely, pressures of 100–200 kg/cm2 fail to provide adequate density and strength, causing crumbling and losses of tablet geometry exceeding 5–15%. Irregular, high-surface-area titanium particles are preferred because they compact at relatively low pressure while retaining the porosity and strength needed for melt absorption. Molasses improves flux adhesion, particle cohesion, and tablet strength; annealing at 80–100 °C burns out 50–60% of the binder while retaining porosity and strength. The excerpt does not provide specific effects of melt stirring or temperature on dissolution time beyond the annealing conditions, nor does it give a separate quantitative dissolution time for optimally compacted tablets.

## pqac-00000041

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 86-92'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes aluminum SPS as a process that promotes particle bonding by overcoming the native oxide film covering each aluminum particle. Aluminum is difficult to sinter conventionally because its stable oxide layer persists at high temperature and limits oxide solubility, producing a long incubation period. Successful sintering therefore requires the oxide films to be disrupted so that clean metal-to-metal contacts can form. SPS combines uniaxial pressure with pulsed direct current and Joule heating in a conductive graphite die. Localized heating at particle interfaces, together with plastic deformation during compaction, is proposed to facilitate oxide-layer fracture or breakdown. High-temperature contact points in SPS/PECS favor oxide disruption more effectively than conventional hot pressing. Pressure contributes by deforming particles, increasing contact area, breaking or displacing oxide films, and enabling stronger metallurgical bonds. Studies cited in the excerpt associate higher pressure at elevated temperature with improved ductility, neck growth, and more uniform sintering. Oxide debris generated during SPS can also improve metal-to-metal contact. The abstract further reports that electrical resistance drops markedly near 0.3 Tm; the area under this drop correlates with ductility, interpreted as evidence that oxide breakdown becomes easier and metallurgical bonding improves at this temperature. Overall, SPS oxide disruption results from the combined effects of current-assisted interfacial heating, pressure-driven plastic deformation, and formation of intimate metallic contacts.

## pqac-00000042

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 109-114'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum as a coupled mechanical and electrical-thermal process. Compaction pressure is considered the primary mechanism: plastic deformation of aluminum particles fractures or disrupts their oxide layers, allowing improved metal-to-metal contact and interface bonding. Increasing pressure from 20 to 50 MPa increased final density, produced near-full density at 50 MPa, and improved ductility, supporting the importance of pressure-driven oxide breakup and contact formation. The applied electrical current enhances this process through Joule self-heating within the powder bed. Localized high temperatures at particle contacts soften the aluminum, making pressure-induced deformation more effective, while electrical-field effects may independently assist oxide disruption. The excerpt also notes that pressure ramping during heating can improve ductility compared with applying constant pressure before heating. This may result from greater electrical-field exposure at lower initial powder density, increased atomic mobility and diffusion, enhanced spark formation or local heating between particles, and reduced gas entrapment. A marked resistance decrease near 200 °C is interpreted as evidence of oxide-layer breakdown and is used to assess the quality of interfaces between aluminum particles. Thus, oxide fracture during compaction is not attributed to pressure alone; pressure, current-assisted heating, local contact conditions, and evolving particle interfaces act together.

## pqac-00000043

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 103-109'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum powder as primarily a mechanically driven process. Aluminum particles possess an inherent oxide layer, and plastic deformation during compaction can fracture or disrupt this film, enabling metal-to-metal contact and particle bonding. Applied pressure is therefore critical: increasing pressure produces greater oxide disruption, more consolidated metal contacts, reduced porosity, higher flexural strength and ductility, and more pronounced dimples on fracture surfaces. At low pressure, particle debonding and limited neck development remain visible; at higher pressure, prior particle boundaries diminish and ductile dimple formation increases. Electrical resistance provides indirect evidence of oxide breakdown and contact formation. Resistance decreases as densification progresses, with a particularly significant reduction near 0.3 Tm, coinciding with enhanced densification and interpreted as increased metal-to-metal bonding after oxide-layer disruption. The oxide film becomes easier to break at elevated temperature, especially above approximately 200 °C, because aluminum softens relative to alumina. Current application is considered to amplify the pressure effect through Joule heating within the powder bed, promoting plastic deformation and oxide fracture. Comparisons at similar density indicate that higher-pressure processing improves bonding and ductility beyond the effect of porosity reduction alone.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt attributes oxide-film disruption during SPS of aluminium powder primarily to pressure-assisted plastic deformation of the relatively soft aluminium particles, rather than confirmed melting and resolidification at particle interfaces. As temperature rises, the hardness ratio of alumina to aluminium increases, while aluminium softens; this makes particle deformation more effective and helps fracture or disrupt the oxide film during compaction. The bonding-interface temperature may exceed the average SPS temperature because of Joule heating, potentially further facilitating oxide disruption. Current concentration at particle contact points may also contribute through electroplasticity, although the excerpt notes that substantial overheating at contacts may not occur for small particles because heat dissipates rapidly. Experimental evidence includes a resistance-curve drop beginning around 200 °C, becoming stronger with increasing pressure, and improved flexural performance and fracture-surface evidence of particle bonding at higher loading pressures. Thus, increasing either SPS pressure at constant temperature or temperature at constant pressure increases the fraction of metal-to-metal interfaces. These newly formed contacts improve particle bonding; subsequent forging further breaks oxide layers and reduces residual porosity.

The excerpt identifies aluminum’s stable native oxide film as the principal obstacle to conventional sintering. Because the oxide has limited solubility in aluminum, effective consolidation requires disruption of the surface film so that clean metal-to-metal contacts can form. Spark plasma sintering is advantageous because simultaneous uniaxial pressure and pulsed electrical current produce rapid Joule heating, particularly at particle interfaces and contact points. During compaction, plastic deformation and the formation of high-temperature contact regions promote oxide-layer breakdown. Fractured or displaced oxide debris can improve subsequent metal-to-metal contact. Increasing pressure, especially at elevated temperatures, enhances particle neck growth, promotes more uniform sintering, and improves ductility, indicating stronger interparticle bonding. The cited studies also associate higher sintering temperatures and applied pressure with improved oxide disruption and bonding; one proposed mechanism involves microplasma generation between particle contacts under pressure and a reduced atmosphere from the carbon mold. The article’s central interpretation is that electrical resistance changes during SPS can indicate this bonding process: a pronounced resistance descent near approximately 0.3 Tm corresponds to easier oxide breakdown and enhanced metallurgical bonding. Thus, pressure contributes mechanically through particle rearrangement, plastic deformation, contact enlargement, and oxide fracture, while SPS heating assists oxide disruption at the newly created interfaces.

## pqac-00000046

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 149-153'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt explains that aluminum powder particles are covered by a stable, tenacious oxide film that inhibits sintering unless metal-to-metal contact is created by disrupting the film. SPS can disrupt the oxide layer and produce good bonding, particularly for inert-gas-atomized aluminum with a relatively thin oxide layer (approximately 3–4 nm), whereas air-atomized powder has a thicker layer (approximately 7 nm) and is more difficult to bond. Increasing oxide thickness reduces the likelihood of sufficient metal-to-metal contact during SPS. Applied pressure or load is important because it promotes particle contact and oxide breakup; in alloy powders containing Mg, a possible Mg–alumina spinel layer may require a higher load to fracture the oxide. The excerpt also identifies forging/upset forging as a secondary process that applies high strains and strain rates, closes residual porosity, and disrupts oxide films at particle interfaces. Once the oxide is broken, enhanced metallurgical bonding can occur. However, the modified Alumix 431D material still exhibited incomplete particle bonding after sintering alone, indicating that SPS pressure and oxide disruption may be insufficient without subsequent forging.

## pqac-00000047

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt identifies the native aluminum oxide film as the principal barrier to powder sintering because it prevents diffusion and metal-to-metal contact between particles. Oxide disruption can occur through several mechanisms: plastic deformation during powder compaction, formation of a liquid phase, cracking during heating, and reactions involving magnesium that produce MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel. However, the mechanical disruption produced by conventional compaction pressure is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering. This implies that pressure may create discontinuities or cracks in the oxide network, but does not normally break it up enough to achieve reliable bonding by itself. Successful aluminum powder sintering therefore often relies on liquid-phase penetration through defects formed during compaction, with suitable wetting and mass transport. Magnesium can further assist by reducing or disrupting the oxide and enabling liquid penetration. In relation to SPS, the excerpt states that pulsed current may provide electropulsing-related benefits, including refined microstructure and potentially improved mechanical properties. It also reports that SPS of pure aluminum has produced good particle bonding by reducing the oxide-layer problem, although bonding difficulties remain possible for some aluminum alloys. The passage does not provide a quantitative pressure dependence or a detailed SPS-specific fracture model.

From text 'tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 98-103'.

MM Tünçay. Evaluation of spark plasma sintering and forging of aluminum based powders for near-net shapes. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt is directly relevant to oxide-film disruption and pressure effects during SPS of aluminum powder. Increasing compaction pressure raises the final relative density, from 0.925 at 20 MPa to 0.984 at 50 MPa, indicating enhanced densification and likely increased opportunities for particle contact. Electrical resistance is high initially and decreases as the powder densifies; the resistance associated with the aluminum powder itself is calculated to be very small compared with the graphite and other tooling components. However, the initial oxide films on aluminum particles can substantially increase powder-bed resistivity, making resistance evolution potentially useful for assessing oxide behavior. The text discusses two possible oxide-disruption mechanisms: dielectric breakdown under locally amplified electric fields and mechanical disruption during plastic deformation. It notes that dielectric breakdown is established for nickel but remains uncertain for aluminum because aluminum oxide has a much higher breakdown strength, approximately 1 × 10^7 V·cm−1. Mechanical deformation is identified as a route for breaking the oxide layer, with oxide films becoming easier to fracture at higher temperatures. The excerpt does not yet provide detailed direct observations of metal-to-metal contact formation or fracture-surface evidence; those appear to be topics developed in the continuation.
