## Compacting Aluminium-Alloy Powder Before Melting for Ultrasonic Atomization: A Literature-Based Assessment

---

### 1. Why Loose or Lightly Packed Aluminium-Alloy Powder Fails to Melt into a Bath

The root cause is the tenacious native oxide shell on every gas-atomised aluminium powder particle. Air-atomised aluminium powder typically carries an amorphous, hydrous alumina (Al₂O₃·3H₂O) layer approximately 50–150 Å (5–15 nm) thick; this layer crystallises to γ-Al₂O₃ above approximately 350 °C but does not dissolve or dissociate (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). Because Al₂O₃ is thermodynamically extremely stable—its equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is of the order of 10⁻⁴³ Pa—simply immersing the powder in a melt at 810–840 °C under argon does not strip the films (pqac-00000000). Each particle therefore remains individually encapsulated; the oxide prevents metal-to-metal contact, blocks diffusion and wetting, and inhibits coalescence even when the aluminium core is above its liquidus (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

**Low thermal conductivity of the powder bed** compounds the problem. Measurements on gas-atomised steel powder beds show effective thermal conductivities below 1/100 of the corresponding solid-metal value—for example, approximately 0.03–0.05 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ versus 13–15 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for solid stainless steels, measured in argon at reduced pressure (pqac-00000037). Although direct aluminium powder data at atmospheric argon pressure were not extracted from these sources, solid aluminium has a conductivity of ~238 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (pqac-00000008), and the powder-bed effective conductivity would be at least one to two orders of magnitude lower, making the powder an effective thermal insulator. Even at higher porosities, compaction was shown to improve conductivity monotonically by increasing the solid fraction and interparticle contact area (pqac-00000007).

**Entrapped gas** in the interparticle voids and in internal porosity within each particle adds buoyancy, reduces the effective density below that of the surrounding melt, and can cause powder agglomerates to float rather than submerge (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000027). Gas expansion upon heating can crack a compact or eject material before consolidation (pqac-00000027).

**Role of Mg in AlSi10Mg versus 4047.** In Mg-bearing aluminium alloys, Mg reacts with the native Al₂O₃ film to form MgO or MgAl₂O₄ spinel. These oxides are *more* refractory than the original amorphous alumina: MgAl₂O₄ is thermally stable and was confirmed by XRD at sintered Al–Mg interfaces (pqac-00000001). While Mg can *assist* sintering by disrupting the alumina and enabling liquid-phase penetration at appropriate concentrations (an optimum around 0.15% Mg was cited in one Al–Sn system), the spinel and MgO that form on the powder surface in storage and during atomisation create a tougher, more chemically resistant shell (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000046). This plausibly explains why AlSi10Mg powder failed to consolidate while 4047 (Al-12Si, no Mg) melted: the 4047 particles retained only the thinner, weaker amorphous Al₂O₃ film, which could crack or be penetrated more readily at the melt temperature.

---

### 2. Does Uniaxial Compaction Fix It, and at What Pressure and Relative Density?

**Compaction pressures and densities.** Uniaxial cold pressing of pure aluminium powder at approximately 246 MPa (80 °C warm pressing) produced a relative density of 94.5% under load, rising to 96.7% after a constant-load hold; at 386 MPa the values were 97.0% and 98.2% respectively (pqac-00000010). A second study reported 92% of theoretical density at 464 MPa and 97.25% at 580 MPa for room-temperature pressing (pqac-00000011). Aluminium powder crosses approximately 85% relative density near 90–100 MPa, at which point porosity begins transitioning from open to closed (pqac-00000014). Under spark-plasma sintering at 500 °C, much lower pressures sufficed: 20 MPa → 92.5%, 30 MPa → 95.2%, 40 MPa → 96.6%, 50 MPa → 98.4% (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015).

**Does particle deformation break the oxide?** The literature is consistent that compaction *cracks* and *displaces* oxide films but does not *remove* them. Plastic deformation of the soft aluminium relative to the rigid alumina creates discontinuities and some metal-to-metal contact; this is enhanced at elevated temperature because the hardness ratio of alumina to aluminium increases and aluminium softens (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). However, "mechanical disruption produced by conventional compaction pressure is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering" (pqac-00000047). Supplementary mechanisms—liquid-phase penetration, Mg-assisted oxide reduction, or current-assisted heating (SPS)—are usually needed for strong particle bonding (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000047). For the user's purpose (remelting, not sintering), even partial oxide cracking should help by improving thermal conductivity and allowing the surrounding melt to penetrate the compact once the aluminium core begins to liquefy.

**Evidence from remelting aluminium briquettes.** Cold-pressed aluminium-alloy machining-chip briquettes with a density of 2.29 g cm⁻³ (about 88% of theoretical) were remelted by induction at approximately 850 °C, producing a metallurgical yield of 94.2% with 2.25% dross (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000021). Properly compacted briquettes typically achieve 80–96% yield depending on density and contamination, with densities of 2.20–2.40 g cm⁻³ identified as optimal for steel-deoxidation applications (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023). In a salt-flux remelting study of aluminium scrap, uncoated loose chips and uniaxially compacted briquettes both achieved coalescence above 97% and yields of 97–100%; compaction had a stronger effect on coalescence than on yield per se (pqac-00000019). However, *over*-compacted briquettes (by moderate-pressure torsion, producing nearly zero internal porosity) showed worse de-coating, more dross, and lower coalescence (pqac-00000020).

**Evidence from foundry alloying tablets.** Titanium-powder alloying tablets for aluminium foundries dissolve in 25–40 minutes at 730–750 °C (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034). The recommended compaction pressure is 25.5–29.8 MPa (250–300 kg cm⁻²) to achieve a density of 2.5–5.0 g cm⁻³, preserving enough interconnected porosity for melt infiltration. Pressures of 350–500 kg cm⁻² (34–49 MPa) were termed "overconsolidated" and gave dissolution times of 35–40 minutes because the aluminium melt could not infiltrate the tablet; conversely, pressures below ~10–20 MPa gave tablets that crumbled, losing 5–15% of their mass (pqac-00000033). This demonstrates a clear density window: too dense impedes dissolution, too porous gives inadequate integrity.

---

### 3. Safety and Quality Risks of Melting a Compact

**Is the "ejects molten metal" warning justified?** Yes, under specific conditions. The aluminium–water explosion literature confirms that violent steam-driven metal ejection requires liquid water enclosed by a compact mass of aluminium at a temperature sufficient for rapid vaporisation and oxidation (pqac-00000026). Sources of moisture in an aluminium-powder compact include:

- **Hydrated oxide on the powder surface:** Air-atomised aluminium powder carries an amorphous hydrous alumina layer, Al₂O₃·3H₂O, which decomposes and releases water vapour above approximately 350 °C (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000028).
- **Adsorbed atmospheric moisture** on high-surface-area powder.
- **Die lubricants**, if used, which decompose into gas during heating.
- **Cutting fluid residues** on recycled chips.

If the compact has closed porosity (relative density above approximately 85–90%), gas generated inside cannot escape and the internal pressure rises until the compact bursts, potentially ejecting molten or semi-molten aluminium. This is precisely the mechanism observed in aluminium PM foam manufacture: blowing-agent decomposition (TiH₂, ZrH₂, CaCO₃) generates gas that expands the compact, and hydrogen can begin evolving while the matrix is still solid, producing cracks perpendicular to the compaction direction (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**How conditions change from green to sintered to hot-pressed:**
- *Green compacts:* Retain the most moisture and hydrated oxide; interconnected porosity at moderate density allows gas venting, but a high-density green compact can trap gas. Dropping a green compact into an existing melt is the highest-risk scenario.
- *Sintered compacts:* Heating to 550 °C burns off organics and decomposes hydrated oxide, reducing the gas inventory substantially (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). However, if sintering closes the remaining pores, the degassing benefit is lost.
- *Vacuum hot-pressed or SPS:* Vacuum processing can desorb gas before the pores close, providing the safest consolidated form—provided the compact is subsequently stored dry and clean.

**Oxide inclusions and nozzle clogging.** Compaction does not eliminate oxide; it fragments the films and redistributes them as dispersed particles within the compact. Common inclusions from aluminium powder include Al₂O₃ films and clusters (which can be several millimetres long), MgO, MgAl₂O₄ spinel, and Al₄C₃ (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). In aluminium filtration practice, inclusions as small as 1–30 µm are targeted for removal (pqac-00000049). With a 0.7 mm nozzle, any particle or agglomerate above approximately 0.2–0.3 mm in its longest dimension poses a clogging risk. Flux treatment can reduce inclusion counts by approximately 70% (pqac-00000055), but fluxes themselves may introduce chloride or fluoride residues.

**Hydrogen pickup.** Molten aluminium absorbs hydrogen from water vapour; hydrogen constitutes approximately 70–90% of the total gas in an aluminium melt (pqac-00000051). Every gram of powder introduces more oxide surface area (and thus more adsorbed water) per unit of metal than bulk material, making hydrogen pickup a particular concern when melting powder-derived charges.

**Recommended mitigation:** Always heat the compact *with* the charge from cold (never drop it into an existing melt), dry or degas the powder before pressing (80–100 °C minimum, or vacuum bake), avoid die lubricants if possible (use die-wall lubrication only), and provide vent paths during heating.

---

### 4. Practical Recipe if Compaction Is Worthwhile

Based on the assembled evidence:

| Parameter | Recommended value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Compaction pressure** | 200–300 MPa cold; or ~100–150 MPa at 80–100 °C | Achieves ~90–95% relative density; above ~85% porosity becomes predominantly closed, improving conductivity without fully sealing the compact (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014) |
| **Target relative density** | 90–95% | Provides good thermal conductivity and structural integrity while preserving enough connected porosity for gas venting; avoids overconsolidation that inhibits melt infiltration (pqac-00000033) |
| **Die-wall vs admixed lubricant** | Die-wall only (e.g. zinc stearate on die walls, wiped on) | Admixed lubricant decomposes into gas and carbonaceous residue during heating, increasing dross and hydrogen pickup. Die-wall lubricant minimises residue in the compact (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) |
| **Degassing / drying** | Dry powder at 80–100 °C for ≥1 hour before pressing; consider vacuum bake at 200–300 °C to decompose hydrated oxide | Removes adsorbed moisture and partially dehydrates the alumina shell (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033) |
| **Vacuum pressing** | Not essential but beneficial for fully degassed compacts; vacuum hot pressing at 300–500 °C and 50–100 MPa produces the most reliable product | Vacuum removes entrapped gas before pore closure; hot pressing at moderate temperature improves oxide cracking (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000042) |
| **Sintering** | Optional; if used, 550 °C in flowing argon or vacuum for 30–60 min | Burns off residual organics and decomposes hydrated oxide; conventional sintering of aluminium is difficult due to oxide inhibition, so this is primarily a degassing step rather than a bonding step (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000019) |
| **Blend with aluminium powder** | Yes—blending alloy powder 1:1 or 2:1 with clean Al powder dilutes the oxide burden and improves compressibility | Reduces the total oxide surface area per unit mass; pure Al particles deform more easily and fill interstices |
| **Compact size** | ≤19 mm diameter, 10–15 mm height to fit between stopper rod and crucible wall | Maximises surface-area-to-volume ratio for melt infiltration while meeting geometric constraints |
| **Placement in charge** | Place compact at bottom of crucible, beneath solid 6063 rod pieces; heat from cold | Ensures the compact is submerged before it can float; avoids dropping into an existing melt (pqac-00000026) |
| **Extra superheat / hold time** | Increase melt set point by 20–40 °C (to ~860–880 °C) and extend hold to ≥5 minutes | Foundry alloying tablets required 25–40 minutes at 730–750 °C; even a well-made aluminium-base compact may need several minutes (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034) |
| **Press force for a 19 mm compact** | At 200 MPa: F = 200 × π × (9.5)² ≈ **56.7 kN (~5.8 tonnes-force)**; at 300 MPa: F ≈ **85.1 kN (~8.7 tonnes-force)** | Achievable with a standard laboratory hydraulic press |

---

### 5. How Compaction Compares with the Alternatives

The following table compares all practical options for preparing 100–350 g aluminium alloy charges.

| Method | Advantages | Disadvantages | Best suited for | Risk of nozzle clogging |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loose powder in cup (current approach) | Simple weighing; cup keeps powder together initially; convenient for composition screening. | Powder bed is thermally insulating; each particle retains a refractory oxide shell; the cup may melt before its contents coalesce, releasing floating agglomerates. Hydrous oxide, moisture, and trapped gas can evolve suddenly. Mg-bearing powder can additionally contain MgO/MgAl₂O₄. | Only low-oxide, readily melting pre-alloyed powder already demonstrated to consolidate—e.g., the successful 4047 case—and only after a separate melt test. | **High.** Oxide films and clusters can range from micrometres to millimetres, whereas the nozzle is only 0.7 mm; powder-derived Al₂O₃, MgO, or spinel may remain suspended (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000053). |
| Cold-pressed freestanding compact | Raises bulk density, thermal conductivity, strength, and probability of submergence; particle deformation cracks some oxide films. Aluminium powders reached about 94.5–97.0% relative density under load at 246–386 MPa in warm-compaction tests. | Pressing cracks but does not remove oxide; closed porosity can trap gas. Excessive density can inhibit melt infiltration, while low pressure gives weak compacts. No direct evidence guarantees complete dissolution during a 2 min hold. | Initial screening of 4047/6063 or Al-rich blends; use moderate density rather than maximum density, heat from cold beneath solid charge, and validate before atomization. | **Medium–high.** Better than loose powder, but all particle-surface oxide remains in the charge as fragments or networks; filtration literature targets inclusions as small as 1–30 µm (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049). |
| Sintered, vacuum-hot-pressed, or SPS compact | Strongest and most conductive powder-derived slug; heat plus pressure increases oxide rupture and metal-to-metal bonding. SPS at 500 °C gave 92.5–98.4% density at 20–50 MPa. Vacuum processing can desorb gas before pores close. | More equipment and process development; oxide is dispersed, not eliminated. Near-full density can retain closed gas if degassing is inadequate. Conventional sintering alone is difficult because alumina inhibits diffusion. | When powder chemistry cannot be obtained as a cast master alloy and a repeatable, mechanically robust slug is essential; vacuum hot pressing is preferable to lubricant-bearing green pressing. | **Medium.** Lower risk of releasing intact powder agglomerates, but fractured Al₂O₃/MgO/spinel remains as inclusions and can reach the nozzle (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000046). |
| Commercial master-alloy additions (e.g., Al–50Si, Al–20Si, Al–50Mg, Al–50Cu) | Cast metallic pieces melt or dissolve much more predictably than powder; low surface-area-to-volume ratio minimizes oxide introduced per gram of alloying element. | Compact inside cup with vented sliding plug | Combines improved powder thermal contact with an aluminium envelope; a freely sliding, positively vented plug can maintain containment while permitting gas escape. | If the cup melts before the core, the assembly reverts to a floating compact. A press-fit or obstructed 1 mm vent can behave as a pressure vessel once molten metal seals it; moisture, hydrated oxide, or lubricant can cause rapid gas evolution and metal ejection. | Only as a staged cold-charge experiment with dry, lubricant-free powder, moderate compaction, an unobstructed vent path, and the assembly buried beneath solid feed—not dropped into an existing bath. | **Medium–high.** Better containment than loose powder, but failure of the envelope can release the compact’s oxide inventory abruptly; the safety consequence of blocked venting is also greater (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). |


*Table: Comparison of charge-preparation routes for 100–350 g aluminium melts, emphasizing dissolution reliability, oxide and gas risks, and compatibility with a 0.7 mm atomizer nozzle.*

**Recommendation hierarchy:**

1. **First choice: commercial master alloys.** For Si, Mg, Cu, and Mn—the most commonly adjusted elements—cast master alloys (Al-50Si, Al-20Si, Al-50Mg, Al-50Cu, Al-10Mn, etc.) dissolve predictably at 810–850 °C, introduce minimal oxide per gram of alloy addition, and are available in small pieces that fit the crucible. Al-50Si has been documented for making small-batch Al-Si melts at 850 °C (pqac-00000057). This avoids the powder-melting problem entirely.

2. **Second choice: arc-melted master-alloy button.** When the desired composition or blend is not commercially available (e.g. multi-element blends for novel alloy development), weigh out the powders, arc-melt them into a dense button under argon (with multiple flips), and add the button to the crucible charge as a cast piece. This is a well-established laboratory practice for titanium, nickel, and high-entropy alloys and can be adapted to aluminium. *Note: this recommendation is an engineering extrapolation; no cited aluminium-specific study directly validated it.*

3. **Third choice: cold-pressed compact,** used as an intermediate step when neither master alloys nor arc melting are available or practical. Press at 200–300 MPa (or warm press at 100–150 MPa and 80–100 °C) targeting 90–95% relative density. Dry the powder beforehand, use die-wall lubricant only, place the compact beneath solid charge pieces, heat from cold, and extend the hold time to at least 5 minutes. Validate with the quick test described in Section 6.

4. **When a pressed compact is the *wrong* choice:** (a) When the powder is heavily oxidised, Mg-rich, or moisture-contaminated and cannot be adequately dried; the compact will trap gas and eject. (b) When the target composition is available as a cast master alloy or pre-alloyed wire. (c) When atomisation quality demands are very tight and any oxide inclusion could clog the 0.7 mm nozzle—in this case, cast alloy + degassing is safer.

---

### 6. A Quick Test Before Committing an Atomiser Run

The following screening protocol requires only a laboratory furnace, a small graphite or alumina crucible, an analytical balance, and sectioning/polishing equipment:

1. **Press three compacts** of the target powder blend at 200, 250, and 300 MPa (19 mm diameter). Record mass, dimensions, and density.

2. **Prepare crucible melts.** In each of three small graphite crucibles, load approximately 50 g of 6063 alloy pieces. Place one compact at the bottom of each crucible, beneath the 6063 pieces.

3. **Heat in a resistance furnace** under flowing argon (or in the atomiser's induction module if convenient) to 860 °C. Hold for 5 minutes after the thermocouple reaches set point. If a compact has not merged with the melt in 5 minutes, extend to 10 minutes for comparison.

4. **Cool in the crucible** and section the solidified ingot longitudinally.

5. **Assess:**
   - **Visual:** Is the compact boundary visible? Are there unmolten powder regions, oxide veins, or macro-porosity?
   - **Macro-etch:** A 10% NaOH etch reveals grain flow and dissolution fronts.
   - **SEM/EDS:** Map Si, Mg, Cu (or other target elements) across the section. A successful melt-in produces a homogeneous composition profile; failure leaves a composition step at the former compact boundary.
   - **Weigh dross:** Collect surface oxide and dross; report as a percentage of total charge.

6. **Pass/fail criteria:**
   - ✅ Compact fully incorporated, no macro-porosity, composition uniform within ±0.5 wt% of target across the section.
   - ⚠️ Compact partially dissolved, visible but diffuse boundary, acceptable for a longer hold time.
   - ❌ Compact remains as a distinct region, oxide vein visible, or unmelted powder core present—do not use in an atomiser run.

This test directly mimics the crucible environment (graphite, argon, induction heating) and can be completed in a single day. It avoids wasting an atomiser run on an unproven charge design.

---

### Basis and Limitations of Evidence

The conclusions above draw on direct evidence from aluminium systems except where noted. The oxide-shell barrier mechanism, compaction pressure–density relationships, foundry alloying-tablet dissolution data, aluminium briquette remelting yields, and inclusion/hydrogen concerns are all from aluminium-specific literature. The thermal-conductivity-of-powder-bed data are from steel powders but are physically analogous; the expected ratio for aluminium powder beds is consistent with theoretical models fitted to aluminium data (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). The arc-melting recommendation is an engineering extrapolation from practice with other metals. The steam-explosion evidence is from aluminium–water interaction studies in nuclear-safety contexts (pqac-00000026). No literature was found describing exactly the user's scenario—remelting a pressed aluminium-powder compact in a small induction furnace for ultrasonic atomisation—so the recommendations integrate evidence from the closest analogues: PM aluminium sintering, aluminium scrap briquette remelting, and foundry alloying-tablet dissolution.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that loose aluminium powder does not readily melt into a continuous mass because each air-atomized particle is covered by a persistent oxide film. Air-atomized aluminium powder typically has an oxide layer about 50–150 Å thick; the oxide is initially amorphous and hydrous (Al2O3·3H2O), and can crystallize to γ-Al2O3 during heating above 350°C. During atomization, oxide forms on droplet surfaces, changes their surface energy, inhibits spheroidization, and oxide fragments may become trapped inside particles. Most importantly for consolidation, oxide-covered surfaces do not weld together effectively: the oxide prevents direct metal-to-metal contact and can leave micropores where particle surfaces fail to bond. Thus, the oxide shell acts as a diffusion/contact barrier to melting, wetting, coalescence, and pore elimination. The excerpt does not discuss MgO, MgAl2O4 spinel, or how magnesium concentration changes oxide-shell stability. Therefore, it supports the general role of Al2O3 as a barrier but provides no direct evidence for Mg-dependent shell stabilization or transformation; those aspects require another source.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the native oxide shell on aluminium powder as the principal obstacle to consolidation. The shell is tenacious and inhibits diffusion between neighbouring aluminium particles, preventing the metal-to-metal contact needed for bonding. Aluminium oxide is also thermodynamically very stable; reducing it requires an extremely low oxygen partial pressure (about 10^-43 Pa), so simply heating loose powder in an aluminium melt does not readily eliminate the barrier. Mechanical deformation during ordinary powder compaction can crack or disrupt the oxide only partially and is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering. Other possible disruption mechanisms include cracking during heating, liquid penetration through discontinuities, and chemical reaction with magnesium. Mg can react with the aluminium oxide shell to form MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel, thereby creating discontinuities or reducing the oxide and allowing a liquid phase to penetrate to the underlying aluminium. This improves wetting, particle bonding, and sinterability. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative Mg-content dependence or explicitly compare the stability of Al2O3, MgO, and MgAl2O4 as Mg concentration changes. It does, however, indicate that an effective Mg level depends on oxide volume; in an Al-Sn example, 0.15% Mg was reported as optimal, while insufficient Mg left poor sintering and liquid exudation.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the persistent oxide film surrounding aluminium powder particles as the principal obstacle to consolidation. Because the tenacious oxide shell prevents effective sintering and limits metal-to-metal contact, particles do not readily bond or coalesce even when compacted. Conventional sintering is generally insufficient to disrupt this film; liquid-phase sintering is preferred because a liquid can penetrate and wet the particle surfaces once the oxide barrier is chemically weakened. Magnesium acts as a sintering aid by reducing Al2O3 and forming MgO, whose lower free energy enables disruption of the alumina barrier and improves liquid wetting. The text therefore supports the view that oxide shells act as physical and chemical barriers to melting-related contact, wetting, and coalescence. It also emphasizes that pressure, plastic deformation, and localized Joule heating can break down oxide films and increase metal-to-metal interfaces. However, this excerpt does not specifically describe loose powder added directly to an aluminium melt, nor does it detail MgAl2O4 spinel formation or quantify how Mg concentration affects shell stability. Its evidence is strongest for Al2O3 persistence, Mg-assisted oxide reduction, and mechanically assisted shell disruption during SPS and forging.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that thermal conductivity in porous powder materials is controlled primarily by the amount of solid material and the quality or area of interparticle contacts. In a loose aluminium powder bed, particles have only small contact areas and much of the volume is air-filled, so heat conduction through the solid network is strongly reduced; the air contribution is also very small compared with metallic conduction. The proposed model represents effective thermal conductivity as decreasing with normalized porosity, from the conductivity of fully dense material (κ0) toward the conductivity of air (κair) as porosity approaches its maximum. At 20 °C, air has a thermal conductivity of only 0.026 W·m−1·K−1, while aluminium’s conductivity is much higher. Compaction improves thermal conductivity by reducing porosity and increasing the solid fraction and interparticle contact area, thereby creating better continuous pathways for heat flow. At low residual porosity, the model predicts approximately linear improvement with decreasing porosity. The excerpt does not provide a specific numerical comparison between loose and solid aluminium powder beds, but it supplies the physical mechanism and model describing why compaction raises conductivity.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a numerical comparison specifically for loose aluminium powder beds and solid aluminium. It does, however, describe the general heat-transfer behavior relevant to particulate metal beds. A loose powder bed contains substantial pore space, and the gas in those pores generally conducts heat less effectively than the solid material. Consequently, the effective thermal conductivity of a porous powder bed is expected to be lower than that of a continuous solid, with the extent depending on porosity, apparent density, particle arrangement, gas pressure, and particle-to-particle contact. Vibration or mechanical compaction increases apparent density and reduces porosity. This shifts heat transfer toward conduction through the solid particle network and generally improves the bed’s effective thermal conductivity. The excerpt also notes that particle size and contact effects can be competing factors: finer particles may fill pores and create more contact area, but increased particle contacts can introduce thermal contact resistance. Therefore, compaction generally improves conductivity primarily by reducing void volume and strengthening the solid conduction pathways, but the final value depends on the powder’s structure and operating conditions. No aluminium-specific conductivity values or percentage improvement are given in this passage.

The fitted conductivity parameter for aluminium was 231.71 W/(m·K), close to the cited fully dense pure-aluminium reference value of 238 W/(m·K). contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that unreinforced aluminium powders—both pure Al and Alumix 13—reached high relative densities above 90%, specifically greater than 0.95, when compacted in the reported pressure range of up to approximately 250–386 MPa. Thus, pressures in this range are associated with achieving a relative density above 90% for the aluminium powders. The excerpt does not provide a detailed numerical pressure-versus-density table or individual density values at each intermediate pressure, so an exact pressure threshold for crossing 90% cannot be determined from these pages alone. It does distinguish the unreinforced powders from the composite: Alumix 13 reinforced with 15 wt.% Safﬁl short fibres achieved a lower final relative density of 0.86 under the same general compaction study. The article reports that the Konopicky relationship fitted the densification data well for all three materials, while the Arzt model agreed well only up to approximately D ~ 0.85. Therefore, the directly supported result is that high-density unreinforced aluminium compacts (>0.95 relative density) were obtained at compaction pressures reaching roughly 250–386 MPa, but intermediate pressure-density points require additional data from the full article.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports two uniaxial cold-compaction conditions for aluminium powder. A compaction pressure of 580 MPa produced a measured green-compact density of 2.624 g/cm³, corresponding to 97.25% of aluminium’s theoretical density of 2.698 g/cm³. Reducing the pressure to 464 MPa produced a measured density of 2.618 g/cm³, corresponding to 92% of theoretical density. Thus, both tested pressures achieved a relative density above 90%, while 580 MPa gave the higher relative density. The text notes that the first result, approximately 97%, was slightly higher than the 90–95% range reported in other work, whereas the second result, approximately 92%, fell within that range. These results apply to green aluminium powder compacts produced using an Autopallet Press Machine; the excerpt does not provide a broader pressure–density curve or identify a precise minimum pressure below 464 MPa for exceeding 90% relative density.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that aluminium powder reaches approximately 0.85 relative density at pressures up to about 90–100 MPa. At around this pressure, the compaction behavior changes because the powder enters the final densification stage and porosity becomes closed. Therefore, achieving a relative density above 90% requires pressures higher than approximately 100 MPa, but the excerpt does not provide the exact pressure corresponding to 90% or the complete pressure–density data needed to specify the density at each pressure. The experiments used controlled loading followed by a constant-load period, generally at approximately 241–245 MPa, with one test at 386 MPa. Most densification occurred during the pressure-increase stage; the subsequent constant-load period produced only a small additional density increase, attributed to expulsion of trapped gas rather than creep. Note that although the question refers to cold compaction, the primary experiments described here were conducted at 80 °C, while the comparative reference test was performed at approximately 22 °C. Exact final relative densities at 241–245 and 386 MPa would need to be obtained from the article’s tables or figures, which are not included in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report measured thermal-conductivity values specifically for a loose aluminium powder bed, nor does it provide a direct numerical comparison between the effective conductivity of such a bed and that of solid aluminium. It explains that air conduction must be included in thermal models of porous powder materials, especially at high porosity, because the solid interparticle contact area is small. At 20 °C, the thermal conductivity of air is given as 0.026 W·m−1·K−1, increasing to 0.052 W·m−1·K−1 at 400 °C. The article notes that aluminium’s solid-to-air thermal-conductivity ratio is approximately 9.1 × 10^3, while its electrical ratio is much larger (7.1 × 10^21), motivating separate treatment of air in thermal analysis. The proposed model approaches the solid-material conductivity at zero porosity and the air conductivity at the maximum porosity. However, the excerpt says the air contribution is generally negligible relative to metallic conductivity and experimental uncertainty, except that it becomes relevant at high porosity. Coated and uncoated sheets were shredded into similarly sized chips; some chips were left loose, while others were formed into 20 g briquettes using uniaxial compression, moderate-pressure torsion (MPT), or hot MPT at 450 °C. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that compaction has a much stronger effect on coalescence than on metallurgical metal yield. For uncoated aluminum, loose chips and compacted briquettes all show very high coalescence and yields: average coalescence is about 97% for loose chips and approximately 99–100% for uniaxial, MPT, and hot-MPT briquettes, with yields around 97–100%. For coated aluminum, loose chips have poor average coalescence without thermal treatment (64%) but improve to 96% after thermal treatment; compacted samples generally coalesce better, especially when thermally treated. Average coated values are approximately 40–64% coalescence for untreated compacted routes and 98% for thermally treated uniaxial and hot-MPT briquettes, although MPT results are more variable. Despite these large coalescence differences, coated-metal yields remain relatively similar, roughly 95–99%, while uncoated yields are about 97–100%. Thus, higher compaction/briquette density primarily promotes metal bead coalescence and reduces apparent oxidation-related degradation, rather than producing a large change in measured yield. Coated untreated material develops darker, rougher recovered surfaces because of spontaneous combustion. Since organic content was below 2%, recovery and metal yield differ by only about 1–2%.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that briquette density strongly affects aluminium recovery during remelting, although it does not provide a direct numerical metal-yield or recovery percentage for loose chips versus compacted briquettes. Low-density compaction showed no tangible effect, whereas high-density briquettes produced by moderate-pressure torsion limited de-coating efficiency and metal coalescence. The densest briquettes generated significantly more dross during remelting, implying greater aluminium losses and lower metallurgical yield than loose or less-compacted material. Coated scrap produced approximately two to three times more dross than uncoated aluminium, depending on the compaction treatment. Thermal de-coating did not eliminate this difference effectively: the change in dross between de-coated and non-de-coated compacted materials was only about ±2 wt%, attributed to carbonaceous residues remaining after treatment. Although dense briquettes emitted less than half the CO2 and CO during de-coating, restricted gas transport and incomplete organic removal apparently increased oxidation-related losses and reduced metal coalescence. The introduction also notes that earlier work found high MPT compaction to limit both de-coating and metal coalescence, while lower-density briquetting did not affect recycling in salts. Thus, the available text supports a qualitative conclusion: high-density compaction worsens remelting recovery through increased dross formation and poorer coalescence, while low-density compaction is comparatively neutral. Exact yield values require the article’s experimental results or tables beyond this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports remelting performance for a cold-pressed aluminum scrap briquette, but it does not provide a direct experimental comparison with loose chips. Briquette A had a density of 2.29 g·cm⁻³ and 12.1% porosity. After induction remelting at approximately 850 °C, Sample B formed a compact casting with a density of 2.388 g·cm⁻³, 8.15% porosity, and approximately 91.85% compaction relative to the assumed alloy density of 2.60 g·cm⁻³. The increase in density and reduction in porosity indicate that remelting eliminated gaps between chips and converted the briquetted feedstock into a continuous metallic volume, improving coalescence. From 290.25 g of briquette input, 273.41 g of casting was recovered, corresponding to a metallurgical metal yield of approximately 94.20%. The reported oxide-residue/dross fraction was 2.25%, while the stated overall weight loss was 10.3 g. The remaining porosity was attributed mainly to hydrogen and gases from oil or emulsion decomposition, while oxidation of recycled chip surfaces contributed to dross formation. The excerpt cites 90–96% as typical yield for recycled briquettes with minor oil and oxide contamination, but gives no equivalent yield for uncompacted loose chips.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns gas generation and retention during heating of compacted aluminum powder containing chemical foaming agents, rather than moisture-related safety incidents or steam explosions. It states that CaCO3 decomposes into solid CaO and gaseous CO2 at approximately the aluminum melting temperature, while ZrH2 and TiH2 decompose to release hydrogen. Gas forms foam cells only when it remains trapped within the aluminum matrix. Heating conditions strongly affect gas behavior: at excessively high temperatures, the aluminum matrix melts, flows within the mold, and allows gas to escape more readily, producing weaker foaming and potentially leaving a dense lower region. Prolonged exposure to excessive temperature causes cells to merge into larger cells, which reduces mechanical strength locally. The excerpt also notes that CO2 reacting with aluminum forms an Al2O3 layer on cell walls, helping prevent cell collapse during cooling. These observations are relevant to understanding hazards associated with gas evolution, expansion, and ejection from heated aluminum compacts, but the passage does not directly discuss wet or porous aluminum additions, hydrogen safety, oxide hydration, water-to-steam explosions, or the specific consequences of introducing moisture into molten aluminum.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss moisture, wet aluminium, oxide hydration, or steam explosions when aluminium powder compacts are added to molten aluminium. It does, however, identify mechanisms relevant to gas-related safety risks. Poorly densified powder compacts retain interconnected open porosity, allowing hydrogen to escape rather than producing controlled internal bubbles. Gas can also be lost through cracks in the solid precursor and by bubble coalescence with the atmosphere. Conversely, compaction at 500°C or above can cause premature hydrogen evolution, indicating that heating conditions may release gas before the metal is fully molten or structurally capable of containing it. The excerpt also notes that only part of the hydrogen in TiH2 is released during aluminium foaming and that residual blowing agent remains after processing. In molten metal, solid oxide particles or other solid alloy constituents can destabilize cell walls and initiate rupture. These observations support concern about rapid gas release, trapped or expanding gas, cracking, and ejection during melting, but they do not establish the specific consequences of water contamination or provide a quantified steam-explosion hazard assessment. Moisture-related conclusions would require additional sources addressing water-to-steam conversion and molten-aluminium reactions.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses the steam-explosion hazard when water or moisture is trapped within or enclosed by molten aluminum. In cited aluminum–water experiments, violent explosions required liquid water to become enclosed by a compact mass of aluminum and an aluminum temperature high enough to cause rapid, essentially explosive water vaporization, followed by rapid oxidation of the newly formed metal particles. Thus, wet, porous, or otherwise gas- or moisture-containing aluminum added to molten aluminum could create a sudden steam-generation and molten-metal dispersal event if the moisture is confined and heat transfer is rapid. The severity depends on the quantity of simultaneously reacting metal, the specific surface area of particles, metal temperature, water depth, stream geometry, and whether the metal forms a compact mass. Conditions that cool or disperse the aluminum reduce the likelihood of the described violent mechanism, while high temperature and confinement promote it. The passage does not specifically discuss hydrogen evolution, hydrated oxide decomposition, trapped non-water gas expansion, or oxide hydration during remelting, although it notes uncertainty about participating reactions and identifies rapid oxidation as part of the explosion sequence. It also indicates that molten-metal dispersal itself may be significant in reactor environments.

Laboratory alumina tablets were deliberately manufactured with differing impurity contents while maintaining similar physical properties, allowing chemical composition effects to be isolated. The tablets used high-purity tabular and calcined alumina powders with additions of silica, soda ash, and magnesium oxide. Polyvinyl alcohol binder was added to improve green strength, and the mixture was pressed at 30 tons into 32 mm diameter, 10 mm thick discs, then dried and sintered at 1600°C for five hours. The resulting tablets had approximately 15% apparent porosity; this is relevant to compact density, permeability, and potentially dissolution or reaction kinetics, though no dissolution rate is given. After sintering, samples were cut into 10 mm cubes for molten-metal experiments. The study used molten aluminium velocities of 0.0 mm/s (static), 1.8 mm/s (average plant velocity), and 3.6 mm/s, providing conditions relevant to stirring or forced flow. Temperatures included 690°C and 715°C, with plant casting temperatures reported as 680–720°C. These parameters could support comparisons of melt temperature and fluid motion effects, but the excerpt concerns alumina/aluminium reactions rather than titanium additions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies compact density and porosity as major controls on titanium alloying-tablet dissolution in aluminium melt. The recommended tablet density is 2.5–5.0 g/cm3, obtained at an optimum compaction pressure of 250–300 kg/cm2 (25.5–29.8 MPa). Excessive pressure, 350–500 kg/cm2, can fracture titanium powder particles internally. During melting, aluminium can penetrate these voids, allowing flux–metal interaction and oxide formation, which ultimately becomes slag. Overconsolidated briquettes have insufficient porosity, so the moving aluminium melt cannot infiltrate them fully; they may form a barrier oxide layer and dissolve slowly, with a reported dissolution rate of 35–40 minutes. Conversely, pressures of 100–200 kg/cm2 fail to provide adequate density and strength, causing crumbling and losses of tablet geometry exceeding 5–15%. Irregular, high-surface-area titanium particles are preferred because they compact at relatively low pressure while retaining the porosity and strength needed for melt absorption. Molasses improves flux adhesion, particle cohesion, and tablet strength; annealing at 80–100 °C burns out 50–60% of the binder while retaining porosity and strength. The excerpt does not provide specific effects of melt stirring or temperature on dissolution time beyond the annealing conditions, nor does it give a separate quantitative dissolution time for optimally compacted tablets.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that titanium alloying tablets dissolve in aluminium melt in approximately 25–30 minutes at operating melt temperatures of 730–750 °C. Their dissolution behavior is linked to tablet porosity, strength, density, and the area of contact with the melt. Density is controlled by compacting pressure; as compaction increases, contact area can grow while the influence of internal pores during melting decreases. The study evaluates dissolution kinetics experimentally by melting A7E aluminium at 730–740 °C and sampling the melt at intervals from 2 to 40 minutes. The tablets reportedly dissolve 15–20% faster than comparable products. The alloying briquettes contain titanium powder and Ti80F20 flux, while molasses is used as a binder to improve powder compressibility, flux adhesion, mechanical strength, and uniform flux distribution. Uniform flux distribution and homogeneous pores are presented as beneficial for dissolution and for achieving the intended aluminium-alloy intermetallic structure. The excerpt does not provide detailed evidence about mechanical stirring, nor does it explicitly discuss overconsolidated briquettes as a separate dissolution problem; it only indicates that compaction pressure, porosity, and density affect melting behavior.

Laboratory-made alumina tablets had approximately 15% open porosity, fine grains of about 20 µm, and lower sintering temperature than commercial alumina. These features allowed magnesium to penetrate rapidly from the surface toward the tablet core, producing faster conversion of alumina and embedded impurities into Mg-spinel than in denser commercial alumina granules. Thus, compact porosity, grain size, and consolidation or sintering conditions are important factors governing melt penetration and reaction kinetics. Dynamic tests were performed with a 5% Mg–Al alloy at 715°C and a relative velocity of 1.8 mm/s; a 36-hour contact example is shown. contexts.context: The excerpt describes aluminum SPS as a process that promotes particle bonding by overcoming the native oxide film covering each aluminum particle. Aluminum is difficult to sinter conventionally because its stable oxide layer persists at high temperature and limits oxide solubility, producing a long incubation period. Successful sintering therefore requires the oxide films to be disrupted so that clean metal-to-metal contacts can form. SPS combines uniaxial pressure with pulsed direct current and Joule heating in a conductive graphite die. Localized heating at particle interfaces, together with plastic deformation during compaction, is proposed to facilitate oxide-layer fracture or breakdown. High-temperature contact points in SPS/PECS favor oxide disruption more effectively than conventional hot pressing. Pressure contributes by deforming particles, increasing contact area, breaking or displacing oxide films, and enabling stronger metallurgical bonds. Studies cited in the excerpt associate higher pressure at elevated temperature with improved ductility, neck growth, and more uniform sintering. Oxide debris generated during SPS can also improve metal-to-metal contact. The abstract further reports that electrical resistance drops markedly near 0.3 Tm; the area under this drop correlates with ductility, interpreted as evidence that oxide breakdown becomes easier and metallurgical bonding improves at this temperature. Overall, SPS oxide disruption results from the combined effects of current-assisted interfacial heating, pressure-driven plastic deformation, and formation of intimate metallic contacts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum as a coupled mechanical and electrical-thermal process. Compaction pressure is considered the primary mechanism: plastic deformation of aluminum particles fractures or disrupts their oxide layers, allowing improved metal-to-metal contact and interface bonding. Increasing pressure from 20 to 50 MPa increased final density, produced near-full density at 50 MPa, and improved ductility, supporting the importance of pressure-driven oxide breakup and contact formation. The applied electrical current enhances this process through Joule self-heating within the powder bed. Localized high temperatures at particle contacts soften the aluminum, making pressure-induced deformation more effective, while electrical-field effects may independently assist oxide disruption. The excerpt also notes that pressure ramping during heating can improve ductility compared with applying constant pressure before heating. This may result from greater electrical-field exposure at lower initial powder density, increased atomic mobility and diffusion, enhanced spark formation or local heating between particles, and reduced gas entrapment. A marked resistance decrease near 200 °C is interpreted as evidence of oxide-layer breakdown and is used to assess the quality of interfaces between aluminum particles. Thus, oxide fracture during compaction is not attributed to pressure alone; pressure, current-assisted heating, local contact conditions, and evolving particle interfaces act together.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the native aluminum oxide film as the principal barrier to powder sintering because it prevents diffusion and metal-to-metal contact between particles. Oxide disruption can occur through several mechanisms: plastic deformation during powder compaction, formation of a liquid phase, cracking during heating, and reactions involving magnesium that produce MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel. However, the mechanical disruption produced by conventional compaction pressure is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering. This implies that pressure may create discontinuities or cracks in the oxide network, but does not normally break it up enough to achieve reliable bonding by itself. Successful aluminum powder sintering therefore often relies on liquid-phase penetration through defects formed during compaction, with suitable wetting and mass transport. Magnesium can further assist by reducing or disrupting the oxide and enabling liquid penetration. In relation to SPS, the excerpt states that pulsed current may provide electropulsing-related benefits, including refined microstructure and potentially improved mechanical properties. It also reports that SPS of pure aluminum has produced good particle bonding by reducing the oxide-layer problem, although bonding difficulties remain possible for some aluminum alloys. The passage does not provide a quantitative pressure dependence or a detailed SPS-specific fracture model.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes oxide-film disruption during spark plasma sintering of aluminum powder as primarily a mechanically driven process. Aluminum particles possess an inherent oxide layer, and plastic deformation during compaction can fracture or disrupt this film, enabling metal-to-metal contact and particle bonding. Applied pressure is therefore critical: increasing pressure produces greater oxide disruption, more consolidated metal contacts, reduced porosity, higher flexural strength and ductility, and more pronounced dimples on fracture surfaces. At low pressure, particle debonding and limited neck development remain visible; at higher pressure, prior particle boundaries diminish and ductile dimple formation increases. Electrical resistance provides indirect evidence of oxide breakdown and contact formation. Resistance decreases as densification progresses, with a particularly significant reduction near 0.3 Tm, coinciding with enhanced densification and interpreted as increased metal-to-metal bonding after oxide-layer disruption. The oxide film becomes easier to break at elevated temperature, especially above approximately 200 °C, because aluminum softens relative to alumina. Current application is considered to amplify the pressure effect through Joule heating within the powder bed, promoting plastic deformation and oxide fracture. Comparisons at similar density indicate that higher-pressure processing improves bonding and ductility beyond the effect of porosity reduction alone.

It states that aluminum powder particles retain an oxide shell and that retained oxygen and compact porosity can impair the properties of conventionally processed PM aluminum. In the discussion of powder forging, the oxide film on aluminum particles is described as being fractured and dispersed during hot forging; these fine oxide particulates may then act as strengthening agents. This supports the general concept that mechanical deformation can disrupt and redistribute the native oxide film. contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses hydrogen and oxide/non-metallic inclusion removal during aluminium melt treatment, although it does not specifically discuss powder or scrap remelting, casting-quality defects, bifilms, or passage through a small orifice/nozzle. Hydrogen and inclusions can be reduced by flotation or rotary degassing: inert or chemically inactive gases such as argon or nitrogen are introduced as fine bubbles, hydrogen diffuses into the bubbles and is removed at the melt surface, while suspended inclusions attach to rising bubbles and float out. Small bubbles are particularly useful because their high surface-area-to-volume ratio promotes hydrogen transfer and can also remove non-metallic solid particles. Enhanced melt flow improves bubble–inclusion collisions, inclusion agglomeration, and purification. Filtration removes contaminants, trapped oxides, and other second-phase particles as molten aluminium passes through refractory beds, screens, or ceramic foam filters. The stated target particle size range is 1–30 μm. Cake filtration mainly separates larger inclusions, whereas bed filtration removes particles through collision, adhesion, sedimentation, and fluid-dynamic effects. Filter performance depends on porosity, roughness, area, bed length, melt temperature, and flow rate. Bonded ceramic filters reportedly achieve up to 90% removal for 10–25 μm inclusions, while high-porosity ceramic foam filters are more effective for finer particles.

The article emphasizes that inclusion removal also depends on holding time and that fluxes might remain in the melt, although PoDFA did not confirm this. Filtration immediately before casting is used industrially, but minimizing inclusions before filtration is important because they can block the filter. contexts.context: The excerpt is highly relevant to oxide inclusions and filtration of molten aluminum, but it does not specifically address hydrogen content, remelting powder or scrap, bifilm terminology, or flow through a small orifice/nozzle. It states that inclusions can impair surface appearance, mechanical properties, machining, and forming. Inclusions are classified as exogenous, entering from ingots, alloying additions, master alloys, or refractory containment materials, and endogenous, forming through reactions in the metal-handling system such as oxidation, aluminum carbide, and halide formation. Common Al-Mg alloy inclusions include aluminum oxide films and clusters, MgO, MgAl2O4 spinel, aluminum carbide, complex oxides, and TiB2. Inclusion dimensions range from micron-scale particles to alumina films and clusters several millimeters in size, while many products require inclusions below 50 micrometers at several volume parts per million. Deep-bed filtration is described as effective for capturing inclusions below 20 micrometers because of the filter’s large surface area. The alloys described were made by induction melting under an argon shroud, followed by chill casting. Question: We make small batches of aluminium-alloy powder by ultrasonic atomization (AMAZEMET rePOWDER, induction-heated module) and want to know whether pressing our alloying powder into a compact before melting would fix a melting and mixing problem. Please answer from the literature, with citations (DOIs where possible), and give numbers wherever the sources have them.

**Set-up.** Graphite crucible (BN-coated) heated by induction, 10-11 cm deep, with a sealing (stopper) rod down the middle; the melt is bottom-poured through a ~0.7 mm hBN nozzle onto a 40 kHz vibrating molybdenum plate. Argon at a small overpressure (~0.2 bar), 13-20 ppm O2 in the chamber, melt set point 810-840 °C, held about 2 minutes before pouring. Charges are 170-350 g. There is no mechanical stirring; any stirring comes from the induction field.

**Current charge.** A 6063 aluminium cup (19 mm OD, 12.7 mm bore, 57 mm deep) is filled by weight with gas-atomized alloy powder, closed with a press-fit 6063 plug that has a 1 mm vent hole, and melted with solid 6063 rod. Pieces must stay under 20 mm across to fit between the stopper rod and the crucible wall. In one run the core was AlSi10Mg powder, and it did not melt into the bath: the cup melted, but the powder did not consolidate. In another run the core was 4047 (Al-12Si) powder, and it melted. Next we want composition spreads (varying how much 4047 powder goes into 6063, checked by SEM/EDS) and later blends with elemental or master-alloy powders (for example Si, Mg, Cu, Mn, Fe, Ni, Zr, Sc). The problem is that the powder struggles to melt, coalesce and mix into the rest of the melt in the time and temperature available. The equipment maker warned us that powder compressed inside an aluminium cup could eject molten metal when melted, presumably from trapped gas.

**Proposed fix to evaluate.** Use uniaxial die pressing (powder metallurgy) to turn the powder, alone or blended with aluminium powder, into a partly dense compact (a "semi-solid" pellet or slug under 20 mm in diameter), either as pressed (green) or after sintering, warm pressing, hot pressing or vacuum hot pressing, and melt that in the crucible instead of loose powder in a cup.

Please address:

1. **Why loose or lightly packed aluminium-alloy powder fails to melt into a bath** at 810-840 °C under argon: oxide shells (Al2O3, and MgO or MgAl2O4 spinel for Mg-bearing alloys), low thermal conductivity of a powder bed, entrapped gas, poor wetting, floating agglomerates. Does the Mg in AlSi10Mg plausibly explain why its powder failed while 4047 (no Mg) melted?
2. **Does uniaxial compaction fix it, and at what pressure and relative density?** Does particle deformation break the oxide films enough for metal-to-metal contact and coalescence on melting? Use evidence from remelting aluminium powder, chips or swarf (loose versus cold-compacted versus hot-compacted, metal yield or recovery), remelting PM green or sintered compacts, and aluminium foundry alloying tablets or compacts (Mn, Fe, Cr, Ti, Cu, Ni with aluminium powder, with and without flux): their dissolution times versus melt temperature, compact density and stirring. Also the dissolution of Si added as lump, powder or compact to aluminium melts.
3. **Safety and quality risks of melting a compact**: is the "ejects molten metal" warning justified, and under what conditions (closed porosity, hydrated oxide or moisture on the powder, die lubricants, a compact dropped into a melt versus heated up with the charge from cold)? How do these change from green to sintered to hot-pressed? Effects on oxygen and hydrogen in the melt, on oxide films and inclusions that could clog a 0.7 mm nozzle, and on contamination from lubricants or fluxes.
4. **Practical recipe if compaction is worthwhile**: pressure (MPa), target relative density, die-wall versus admixed lubricant, degassing or drying before pressing, vacuum pressing, sintering atmosphere and temperature, whether to blend with aluminium powder, compact size, where in the charge to put it, and how much extra superheat or hold time it needs. What press force does a 19 mm compact need at those pressures?
5. **How it compares with the alternatives** for 100-350 g induction melts aimed at a homogeneous target composition, low oxygen and no nozzle clogging: compacting the powder inside the cup with a vented sliding plug, a freestanding green compact, a sintered or hot-pressed compact, arc-melting a master alloy button first, buying commercial master alloys (for example Al-50Si, Al-20Si, Al-50Mg, Al-50Cu) or pre-alloyed powder, using a flux, or raising the melt temperature and hold time. Which would you recommend, and when would a pressed compact be the wrong choice?
6. **A quick test** that would tell us whether a compact melts in and mixes, before committing an atomizer run.

Please be explicit about which conclusions come from direct evidence for aluminium systems and which are extrapolated from other metals.


## Compacting Aluminium-Alloy Powder Before Melting for Ultrasonic Atomization: A Literature-Based Assessment

---

### 1. Why Loose or Lightly Packed Aluminium-Alloy Powder Fails to Melt into a Bath

The root cause is the tenacious native oxide shell on every gas-atomised aluminium powder particle. Air-atomised aluminium powder typically carries an amorphous, hydrous alumina (Al₂O₃·3H₂O) layer approximately 50–150 Å (5–15 nm) thick; this layer crystallises to γ-Al₂O₃ above approximately 350 °C but does not dissolve or dissociate (ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 53-57, ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 32-36). Because Al₂O₃ is thermodynamically extremely stable—its equilibrium oxygen partial pressure is of the order of 10⁻⁴³ Pa—simply immersing the powder in a melt at 810–840 °C under argon does not strip the films (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45). Each particle therefore remains individually encapsulated; the oxide prevents metal-to-metal contact, blocks diffusion and wetting, and inhibits coalescence even when the aluminium core is above its liquidus (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 199-204).

**Low thermal conductivity of the powder bed** compounds the problem. Measurements on gas-atomised steel powder beds show effective thermal conductivities below 1/100 of the corresponding solid-metal value—for example, approximately 0.03–0.05 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ versus 13–15 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for solid stainless steels, measured in argon at reduced pressure (wei2018thermalconductivityof pages 7-11). Although direct aluminium powder data at atmospheric argon pressure were not extracted from these sources, solid aluminium has a conductivity of ~238 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (montes2025porosityeffecton pages 6-7), and the powder-bed effective conductivity would be at least one to two orders of magnitude lower, making the powder an effective thermal insulator. Even at higher porosities, compaction was shown to improve conductivity monotonically by increasing the solid fraction and interparticle contact area (montes2025porosityeffecton pages 4-6).

**Entrapped gas** in the interparticle voids and in internal porosity within each particle adds buoyancy, reduces the effective density below that of the surrounding melt, and can cause powder agglomerates to float rather than submerge (ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 32-36, ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 25-29). Gas expansion upon heating can crack a compact or eject material before consolidation (ibrahim2005effectofmaterial pages 25-29).

**Role of Mg in AlSi10Mg versus 4047.** In Mg-bearing aluminium alloys, Mg reacts with the native Al₂O₃ film to form MgO or MgAl₂O₄ spinel. These oxides are *more* refractory than the original amorphous alumina: MgAl₂O₄ is thermally stable and was confirmed by XRD at sintered Al–Mg interfaces (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 45-49). While Mg can *assist* sintering by disrupting the alumina and enabling liquid-phase penetration at appropriate concentrations (an optimum around 0.15% Mg was cited in one Al–Sn system), the spinel and MgO that form on the powder surface in storage and during atomisation create a tougher, more chemically resistant shell (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 45-49, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 149-153). This plausibly explains why AlSi10Mg powder failed to consolidate while 4047 (Al-12Si, no Mg) melted: the 4047 particles retained only the thinner, weaker amorphous Al₂O₃ film, which could crack or be penetrated more readily at the melt temperature.

---

### 2. Does Uniaxial Compaction Fix It, and at What Pressure and Relative Density?

**Compaction pressures and densities.** Uniaxial cold pressing of pure aluminium powder at approximately 246 MPa (80 °C warm pressing) produced a relative density of 94.5% under load, rising to 96.7% after a constant-load hold; at 386 MPa the values were 97.0% and 98.2% respectively (moreno2011densificationofal pages 3-4). A second study reported 92% of theoretical density at 464 MPa and 97.25% at 580 MPa for room-temperature pressing (mohtar2008developingcarbonparticle pages 26-33). Aluminium powder crosses approximately 85% relative density near 90–100 MPa, at which point porosity begins transitioning from open to closed (moreno2011densificationofal pages 2-3). Under spark-plasma sintering at 500 °C, much lower pressures sufficed: 20 MPa → 92.5%, 30 MPa → 95.2%, 40 MPa → 96.6%, 50 MPa → 98.4% (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 98-103, tuncay2016evaluationofthe pages 2-3).

**Does particle deformation break the oxide?** The literature is consistent that compaction *cracks* and *displaces* oxide films but does not *remove* them. Plastic deformation of the soft aluminium relative to the rigid alumina creates discontinuities and some metal-to-metal contact; this is enhanced at elevated temperature because the hardness ratio of alumina to aluminium increases and aluminium softens (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 86-92, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 109-114, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 103-109, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 199-204). However, "mechanical disruption produced by conventional compaction pressure is generally insufficient for extensive solid-state sintering" (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45). Supplementary mechanisms—liquid-phase penetration, Mg-assisted oxide reduction, or current-assisted heating (SPS)—are usually needed for strong particle bonding (tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 199-204, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45). For the user's purpose (remelting, not sintering), even partial oxide cracking should help by improving thermal conductivity and allowing the surrounding melt to penetrate the compact once the aluminium core begins to liquefy.

**Evidence from remelting aluminium briquettes.** Cold-pressed aluminium-alloy machining-chip briquettes with a density of 2.29 g cm⁻³ (about 88% of theoretical) were remelted by induction at approximately 850 °C, producing a metallurgical yield of 94.2% with 2.25% dross (baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 16-18). Properly compacted briquettes typically achieve 80–96% yield depending on density and contamination, with densities of 2.20–2.40 g cm⁻³ identified as optimal for steel-deoxidation applications (baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 18-20, baron2026characterizationofcoldpressed pages 9-11). In a salt-flux remelting study of aluminium scrap, uncoated loose chips and uniaxially compacted briquettes both achieved coalescence above 97% and yields of 97–100%; compaction had a stronger effect on coalescence than on yield per se (vallejoolivares2022thermaldecoatingpretreatment pages 8-10). However, *over*-compacted briquettes (by moderate-pressure torsion, producing nearly zero internal porosity) showed worse de-coating, more dross, and lower coalescence (vallejoolivares2023effectsofcompaction pages 1-3).

**Evidence from foundry alloying tablets.** Titanium-powder alloying tablets for aluminium foundries dissolve in 25–40 minutes at 730–750 °C (bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 4-5, bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 1-2). The recommended compaction pressure is 25.5–29.8 MPa (250–300 kg cm⁻²) to achieve a density of 2.5–5.0 g cm⁻³, preserving enough interconnected porosity for melt infiltration. Pressures of 350–500 kg cm⁻² (34–49 MPa) were termed "overconsolidated" and gave dissolution times of 35–40 minutes because the aluminium melt could not infiltrate the tablet; conversely, pressures below ~10–20 MPa gave tablets that crumbled, losing 5–15% of their mass (bazhin2016specificityofthe pages 2-4). This demonstrates a clear density window: too dense impedes dissolution, too porous gives inadequate integrity.

The compaction parameters and expected outcomes are summarised in the following table.

| Compaction method | Pressure (MPa) | Target relative density (%) | Key effect on oxide film | Expected remelting behavior | Source references |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Cold uniaxial pressing—low pressure | ~100 | ~85 | Particle rearrangement and initial plastic deformation create some oxide cracks, but extensive Al-to-Al contact is unlikely; porosity begins changing from interconnected to closed near this density. | Stronger and more conductive than loose powder, but still liable to retain gas, float, fragment, or leave oxide-bound agglomerates; not a reliable endpoint for a two-minute melt hold. | (moreno2011densificationofal pages 2-3, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45) |
| Cold uniaxial pressing—practical starting range | 200–250 | ~90–95 | Greater particle deformation enlarges contacts and mechanically disrupts parts of the oxide shells; compaction alone does not remove the oxide or guarantee metallurgical bonding. | Should heat, submerge, and coalesce substantially better than loose powder. Aluminium powder pressed at 245.6 MPa reached 94.5% density under load and 96.7% after the final hold, although those tests were at 80 °C. | (moreno2011densificationofal pages 3-4, moreno2011densificationofal pages 1-2, moreno2011densificationofal pages 4-6, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 40-45) |
| Cold uniaxial pressing—high pressure | 300–400 | ~95–98 | Extensive particle flattening and contact enlargement produce more oxide rupture and fewer voids; at 386 MPa, aluminium powder reached 97.0% under load and 98.2% after the final hold in an 80 °C test. | High thermal conductivity and good mechanical integrity, but nearly closed porosity can trap gas; excessive density can impede melt infiltration, so this is not automatically superior for dissolution. | (moreno2011densificationofal pages 3-4, moreno2011densificationofal pages 2-3, tuncay2018evaluationofspark pages 103-109) |

Inert-gas-atomized powder with ~3–4 nm oxide bonds more readily than air-atomized powder with ~7 nm oxide. | Produces a robust, highly conductive slug that should melt more like bulk alloy than loose powder.
